items.title: Dobrushin coupling estimate and actual particle-to-Vlasov limit
items.design_state: Complete draft argument recorded; scoped checks and independent review remain pending.
items.statement:
Use $Z=\mathbb T^d\times\mathbb R^d$, $d_Z$, $\mathcal P_1(Z)$ and
$\mathcal W_1$ from [[def-csm-dk-phase-space-wasserstein-one]], and the odd
smooth force $k$ with $A=\|Dk\|_\infty$ and $k(0)=0$ from
[[def-csm-dk-periodic-mean-field-model]]. If $\mu_0,\nu_0\in\mathcal P_1(Z)$,
let $\mu_s,\nu_s$ be their global characteristic evolutions from
[[thm-csm-dk-global-lipschitz-vlasov]]. Then for every $s\in\mathbb R$,

$$\mathcal W_1(\mu_s,\nu_s)\le e^{(1+2A)|s|}\mathcal W_1(\mu_0,\nu_0).$$

For a finite integer $N\ge1$, choose the momentum scale $P_0>0$ and set
$\tau_0=mL/P_0$ as in [[def-csm-dk-periodic-mean-field-model]]. Define
$\Xi_N:Z^N\to(T^*\mathbb T_L^d)^N$ by
$\Xi_N((x_i,v_i)_{i=1}^N)=((Lx_i,P_0v_i)_{i=1}^N)$, where multiplication
by $L$ maps $\mathbb R^d/\mathbb Z^d$ to $\mathbb R^d/L\mathbb Z^d$.
Write $\Phi_t^N$ for the complete flow in physical coordinates and time from
[[thm-csm-dk-finite-n-complete-flow]]. For initial points
$Z_1^0,\ldots,Z_N^0\in Z$, define their dimensionless trajectory by

$$ (Z_i(s))_{i=1}^N:=\Xi_N^{-1}\!\left(\Phi_{\tau_0s}^N\bigl(\Xi_N((Z_i^0)_{i=1}^N)\bigr)\right). $$

Put $\mu_N(s)=N^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^N\delta_{Z_i(s)}$. If $\mu_s$ is the characteristic
evolution from any $\mu_0\in\mathcal P_1(Z)$, then

$$\mathcal W_1(\mu_N(s),\mu_s)\le e^{(1+2A)|s|}\mathcal W_1(\mu_N(0),\mu_0).$$

Finally, a narrowly continuous curve (meaning that $s\mapsto\int g\,d\sigma_s$
is continuous for every bounded continuous $g$) $\sigma_s\in\mathcal P_1(Z)$ with
locally bounded first velocity moments that satisfies the weak Vlasov identity
in [[thm-csm-dk-global-lipschitz-vlasov]] is the characteristic evolution from
its initial law. Thus this weak-solution class is unique. The estimate is for
the periodic second-order phase metric above; it is not Golse's first-order
estimate and does not use a collision or Boltzmann-Grad scaling.
items.strategy: proof_strategy: direct; complete argument is in items/thm-csm-dk-dobrushin-and-particle-limit.md and its proof contract.

items.title: Compact iid empirical convergence and propagation of chaos
items.design_state: Complete draft argument recorded; scoped checks and independent review remain pending.
items.statement:
Let $K\subset Z=\mathbb T^d\times\mathbb R^d$ be compact and let
$\mu_0\in\mathcal P_1(Z)$ be supported in $K$. Take an iid sequence
$(Z_i(0))_{i\ge1}$ with common law $\mu_0$ (iid means a common law and mutual
independence as in [[def-identically-distributed-and-iid-random-variables]]).
Its existence for each $\mu_0$ follows from the countable-kernel construction
[[thm-ionescu-tulcea-construction-of-a-markov-chain]] under the Axiom of Choice.
Let $P_0>0$ be the momentum scale, $\tau_0=mL/P_0$, and
$\Xi_N:Z^N\to(T^*\mathbb T_L^d)^N$ be
$\Xi_N((x_i,v_i)_i)=((Lx_i,P_0v_i)_i)$, with torus multiplication as in
[[def-csm-dk-periodic-mean-field-model]]. If $\Phi_t^N$ is the physical
finite-N flow of [[thm-csm-dk-finite-n-complete-flow]], define the
first $N$ dimensionless trajectories by
$ (Z_i(s))_{i=1}^N:=\Xi_N^{-1}\Phi_{\tau_0s}^N\Xi_N((Z_i(0))_{i=1}^N)$.
Write
$\mu_N(s)=N^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^N\delta_{Z_i(s)}$, and let $\mu_s$ be the global
characteristic evolution from $\mu_0$. For $C=1+2A$, every finite $T>0$ and
$N\ge1$ satisfy

$$\mathbb E\sup_{|s|\le T}\mathcal W_1(\mu_N(s),\mu_s) \le e^{CT}\,\mathbb E\mathcal W_1(\mu_N(0),\mu_0) \le e^{CT}\left(\delta+\frac{D_K}{2}\sqrt{\frac{M_\delta}{N}}\right),$$

where for each $0<\delta\le1$ one may choose a finite Borel partition of
$K$ into $M_\delta\le C_K\delta^{-2d}$ cells of diameter at most $\delta$,
$D_K=\operatorname{diam}_{d_Z}(K)$, and $C_K$ depends only on $K$ and $d$.
Consequently the expected phase-space Wasserstein error tends to zero; choosing
$\delta=N^{-1/(2d+2)}$ gives a bound of order $N^{-1/(2d+2)}$ with a constant
depending on $K,d,T,A$. Almost surely,
$\sup_{|s|\le T}\mathcal W_1(\mu_N(s),\mu_s)\to0$.

For each fixed $k\ge1$ and every bounded Lipschitz $\Psi:Z^k\to\mathbb R$
with the sum metric $d_{Z^k}(z,z')=\sum_{j=1}^k d_Z(z_j,z'_j)$, the law
$f_N^{(k)}(s)$ of the first $k$ particles obeys,
for $N\ge k$ and $|s|\le T$,

$$\left|\int\Psi\,df_N^{(k)}(s)-\int\Psi\,d\mu_s^{\otimes k}\right| \le 2\|\Psi\|_\infty\frac{k(k-1)}{2N} +k\operatorname{Lip}(\Psi)e^{CT}\mathbb E\mathcal W_1(\mu_N(0),\mu_0).$$

Thus every fixed marginal converges to the product law uniformly on bounded
time intervals in bounded-Lipschitz tests, where bounded-Lipschitz means
$\|\Psi\|_\infty<\infty$ and
$\operatorname{Lip}(\Psi)=\sup_{z\ne z'}|\Psi(z)-\Psi(z')|/d_{Z^k}(z,z')<\infty$.
This conclusion is specific to the
compact iid preparation and the smooth $N^{-1}$ mean-field model.
items.strategy: proof_strategy: direct; complete argument is in items/thm-csm-dk-compact-iid-propagation-of-chaos.md and its proof contract.

items.title: Conditional mean-field particle distribution limit
items.design_state: Complete draft argument recorded; scoped checks and independent review remain pending.
items.statement:
Adopt the finite-particle model and compact-support iid preparation of
[[post-csm-dk-mean-field-particle-and-iid-model]], including its stated full
Axiom of Choice for constructing the infinite iid sequence. There are two
separate conditional consequences within that model.

First, if the initial $N$-particle law is a normalized symmetric smooth density
with the rapid momentum tails specified in
[[thm-csm-dk-exact-bbgky]], its evolved marginals satisfy the exact normalized
BBGKY hierarchy for every $1\le k\le N$. This is a finite-$N$ identity and
retains all correlations.

Second, for the compact iid preparation with common law $\mu_0$, for every
fixed $k$ and finite $T$, the first $k$ particle law converges to
$\mu_s^{\otimes k}$ uniformly for $|s|\le T$ in bounded-Lipschitz tests. For
each bounded Lipschitz $\Psi:Z^k\to\mathbb R$ and $N\ge k$, its error is at
most

$$2\|\Psi\|_\infty\frac{k(k-1)}{2N} +k\operatorname{Lip}(\Psi)e^{(1+2A)T} \mathbb E\mathcal W_1(\mu_N(0),\mu_0),$$

where $A=\|Dk\|_\infty$, and the expected initial error tends to zero by the
compact-support estimate of [[thm-csm-dk-compact-iid-propagation-of-chaos]].
This is a deduction from the adopted model and preparation assumptions; it is
not a measured observation, a real-gas approximation, or a Boltzmann-Grad
limit.

items.title: Finite pair dynamics immediately creates correlations
items.design_state: Complete draft argument recorded; scoped checks and independent review remain pending.
items.statement:
Use the finite-N model and units of
[[def-csm-dk-periodic-mean-field-model]]. Let $N=2$, $d\ge1$, mass $m>0$ in
kilograms, side length $L>0$ in metres, and choose a smooth, even, nonconstant
periodic potential $W\in C^\infty(\mathbb T_L^d)$ in joules with force
$K=-\nabla W$ in newtons. Let $\sigma_p>0$ in kilogram-metres per second and
$g_{\sigma_p}(p)=(2\pi\sigma_p^2)^{-d/2}
\exp(-|p|^2/(2\sigma_p^2))$. Let $dq$ be the quotient position volume induced
from Euclidean Lebesgue measure on $[0,L)^d$ and let $dp=\lambda_d$ be
momentum Lebesgue measure as defined from [[def-the-one-dimensional-torus-and-normalized-haar-integral]]. The canonical $N=2$ phase volume is
$d\Gamma_2:=dq_1\,dq_2\,dp_1\,dp_2$ as in
[[thm-csm-dk-exact-bbgky]]. The normalized initial density relative to
$d\Gamma_2$ is

$$F_2^0(q_1,q_2,p_1,p_2)=L^{-2d}g_{\sigma_p}(p_1)g_{\sigma_p}(p_2).$$

The density factorizes into uniform position densities and centered Gaussian
momentum densities. Under the exact smooth periodic finite-particle flow,
the one-particle marginal has $\partial_t f_1(0)=0$, while

$$\partial_tF_2(0)=\frac{1}{2\sigma_p^2} K(q_1-q_2)\cdot(p_1-p_2)F_2^0,$$

which is nonzero on a nonempty open subset of phase space. Thus the evolved
two-particle law fails to remain a product for every sufficiently small
nonzero time. No factorization or chaos assumption is made at positive time.
items.strategy: proof_strategy: direct; complete argument is in items/ex-csm-dk-product-law-develops-correlations.md and its proof contract.

items.title: Cutoff elastic-reflection collision measure and gain
items.statement:
Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ ([[def-countable-choice]]). Under this assumption Lebesgue measure is the completion of Borel measure ([[cor-lebesgue-sigma-algebra-is-the-completion-of-borel-lebesgue-measure]]), and every Lebesgue-measurable integrable class has a Borel representative ([[thm-completion-measurable-functions-have-base-measurable-representatives]]). Write $\lambda_3$ for Lebesgue measure on $\mathbb R^3$ ([[def-lebesgue-measure-and-the-lebesgue-sigma-algebra]]). Fix a positive reference speed $v_0>0$, and put $w_0(v)=1+|v|^2/v_0^2$. Let $X$ be the real vector space of equivalence classes modulo $\lambda_3$-almost-everywhere equality of measurable functions $f:\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R$ with

$$\|f\|_{1,w_0}:=\int_{\mathbb R^3}w_0(v)|f(v)|\,d\lambda_3(v)<\infty.$$

Let $S^2=\{n\in\mathbb R^3:|n|=1\}$. For a Borel set $E\subseteq S^2$, define the normalized finite angular measure

$$\sigma(E):=\frac1{4\pi}\int_0^\pi\int_0^{2\pi}\mathbf 1_E(\sin\theta\cos\phi,\sin\theta\sin\phi,\cos\theta)\sin\theta\,d\phi\,d\theta.$$

For $v,w\in\mathbb R^3$ and $n\in S^2$, define the postcollision velocities

$$v'=v-((v-w)\cdot n)n,\qquad w'=w+((v-w)\cdot n)n.$$

The collision-parameter measure is $d\mu=d\lambda_3(v)\,d\lambda_3(w)\,d\sigma(n)$ on $\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R^3\times S^2$. Its angular factor is finite and normalized; there is no singular angular weight. For $f,g\in X$, choose Borel representatives and define the gain $\mathcal G(f,g)$ by the almost-everywhere integral

$$\mathcal G(f,g)(v):=\int_{\mathbb R^3\times S^2} f(v')g(w')\,d\lambda_3(w)\,d\sigma(n).$$

The value on any exceptional null set is immaterial because the output is an equivalence class. The next item proves that this definition is independent of the representatives, maps $X\times X$ to $X$, and has the stated collision and moment identities.

references.title: David Tong, Kinetic Theory, Part 2
R. Fitzpatrick, Plasma Physics, Boltzmann H-Theorem

items.title: Well-defined elastic reflection gain and collision identities
items.statement:
Let $\mathcal G$, $v'$, $w'$, $X$, $w_0$, and $\mu$ be as in [[def-csm-dk-reflection-collision-gain]]. For $f,g\in X$, the gain is independent of the chosen Borel representatives, is bilinear, and satisfies

$$\|\mathcal G(f,g)\|_{1,w_0}\le 2\|f\|_{1,w_0}\|g\|_{1,w_0}.$$

For $f\ge0$ with finite mass $M=\int f\,dv$ and finite second moment, it also satisfies

$$\int\mathcal G(f,f)\,dv=M^2,\qquad \int v\mathcal G(f,f)\,dv=M\int vf\,dv,\qquad \int |v|^2\mathcal G(f,f)\,dv=M\int |v|^2f\,dv.$$

If $M=1$, set $A=f(v)f(w)$, $B=f(v')f(w')$, and $\Delta\varphi=\varphi(v)+\varphi(w)-\varphi(v')-\varphi(w')$. For every real-valued measurable test $\varphi$ such that

$$\int_{\mathbb R^3}|\varphi(v)|\mathcal G(f,f)(v)\,dv<\infty,\qquad \int_{\mathbb R^3}|\varphi(v)|f(v)\,dv<\infty,\qquad \int |A\Delta\varphi|\,d\mu<\infty,\qquad \int |B\Delta\varphi|\,d\mu<\infty,$$

the following identity holds:

$$\int_{\mathbb R^3}\varphi(v)\bigl(\mathcal G(f,f)(v)-f(v)\bigr)\,dv=\frac14\int (B-A)\Delta\varphi\,d\mu.$$

For each fixed $n$, the map $(v,w)\mapsto(v',w')$ is a linear orthogonal involution, preserves $v+w$ and $|v|^2+|w|^2$, and has Jacobian determinant of absolute value one. The angular measure has full support, hence the product parameter measure $\mu$ has full support on $\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R^3\times S^2$. Every pair $(v,w)$ and $(\widetilde v,\widetilde w)$ with the same momentum and squared-speed sum is related by one such reflection.

references.title: David Tong, Kinetic Theory, Part 2
R. Fitzpatrick, Plasma Physics, Boltzmann H-Theorem

items.title: Kinetic density, velocity, covariance stress and heat flux
items.statement:
Use the velocity space $\mathbb R^3$ and Lebesgue measure $dv$ fixed by [[def-csm-dk-reflection-collision-gain]]. Let $\Omega=\prod_{j=1}^3(\mathbb R/L_j\mathbb Z)$ be a flat periodic spatial domain with periods $L_j>0$ (in metres in the physical interpretation), and let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an open time interval. Let $F:\Omega\times\mathbb R^3\times I\to[0,\infty)$ be a measurable number density in position and velocity. At each $(r,t)$ where the integrals below are finite, assume $0<n(r,t):=\int_{\mathbb R^3}F(r,v,t)\,dv<\infty$ and $\int |v|^3F(r,v,t)\,dv<\infty$. Fix a particle mass $m>0$ in kilograms, with number count dimensionless. In SI, $F$ has units $\mathrm{m}^{-3}(\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}})^{-3}$.

Define $(x\otimes y)_{ij}=x_i y_j$, $\nabla_r\cdot T$ by $(\nabla_r\cdot T)_i=\sum_j\partial_{r_j}T_{ij}$, and $A:B=\sum_{i,j}A_{ij}B_{ij}$. Define the number density $n$, mass density $\rho=mn$, mean velocity $u=n^{-1}\int vF\,dv$, kinetic covariance momentum flux

$$\Pi=m\int_{\mathbb R^3}(v-u)\otimes(v-u)F\,dv,$$

internal kinetic-energy density $e=\tfrac12\operatorname{tr}\Pi$, and heat-flux vector

$$q=\frac m2\int_{\mathbb R^3}|v-u|^2(v-u)F\,dv.$$

Their SI units are respectively $\mathrm{m}^{-3}$, $\mathrm{kg\,m^{-3}}$, $\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$, pascals, $\mathrm{J\,m^{-3}}$, and $\mathrm{J\,m^{-2}\,s^{-1}}$. The tensor $\Pi$ is symmetric because each integrand $(v-u)\otimes(v-u)$ is symmetric, and it is positive semidefinite because for every $\xi\in\mathbb R^3$, $\xi^{\mathsf T}\Pi\xi=m\int[\xi\cdot(v-u)]^2F\,dv\ge0$. It is the kinetic momentum-flux covariance; in the balance law below it enters with a plus sign, while a continuum tensile-stress variable defined from it would be $-\Pi$.

references.title: David Tong, Kinetic Theory, Part 2
R. Fitzpatrick, Plasma Physics, Boltzmann H-Theorem

items.title: Selected phenomenological cutoff collision model
items.statement:
For this selected model, an identical classical particle is nonrelativistic in the explicit sense that its velocity is a vector $v\in\mathbb R^3$ and its kinetic energy is the Newtonian scalar $m|v|^2/2$. The mass $m>0$ is a primitive model parameter in kilograms. At time $t\ge0$, $f_t(v)$ is the probability density of velocity for a randomly selected particle with respect to Lebesgue measure $dv$; it is nonnegative, normalized by $\int f_t\,dv=1$, and therefore has SI units $(\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}})^{-3}$. Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ for the completed Lebesgue measure used by the mathematical gain definition ([[def-countable-choice]]). A positive speed $v_0$ in $\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ is a reference scale used only to make the logarithm in the one-particle information functional dimensionless. The Boltzmann constant $k_B>0$ in $\mathrm{J\,K^{-1}}$ is a primitive conversion factor when that functional is assigned entropy units.

Let $X$ and $w_0(v)=1+|v|^2/v_0^2$ be as defined in [[def-csm-dk-reflection-collision-gain]]. On the interior of a time interval $J\subseteq[0,\infty)$, an admissible classical trajectory is a map $t\mapsto f_t\in X$ continuously differentiable in the $X$ norm, with its derivative extending continuously to included endpoints by one-sided derivatives, and with $f_t\ge0$ almost everywhere and $\int f_t\,dv=1$ for every $t\in J$. Thus each admissible density has finite second velocity moment. The differential equation below is an equality in the normed space $X$, hence an equality of equivalence classes of functions of velocity. When a trajectory has a chosen representative $\widetilde f:J\times\mathbb R^3\to[0,\infty)$ that is continuously differentiable in $t$ and for which the gain integral is finite and continuous in $(t,v)$, the pointwise form $\partial_t\widetilde f(t,v)=\lambda(\mathcal G(\widetilde f_t,\widetilde f_t)(v)-\widetilde f(t,v))$ is required for every $(t,v)$ on that representative; this pointwise conclusion is not asserted for arbitrary representatives of an $X$ class.

Adopt the spatially homogeneous kinetic equation

$$\frac{d}{dt}f_t=\lambda\bigl(\mathcal G(f_t,f_t)-f_t\bigr)\quad\text{in }X,\qquad \lambda>0,$$

where $\mathcal G$ and the elastic reflection $(v,w)\mapsto(v',w')$ are exactly those of [[def-csm-dk-reflection-collision-gain]] and [[lem-csm-dk-reflection-measure-and-gain-identities]]. The angular measure is the finite normalized area law specified there, and $\lambda$ is a prescribed rate in $\mathrm{s^{-1}}$, independent of relative speed; it is not a measured cross-section or a derived microscopic frequency. The selected incoming pair law is $f(v)f(w)\,dv\,dw$, and the gain uses the corresponding product $f(v')f(w')$ after reflection. This factorized independent-pair closure is adopted here; it is not deduced from reversible many-particle mechanics or from a molecular-chaos theorem. The mathematical existence and regularity claims are separate from this physical adoption.

The model's global mild evolution and its finite-energy hypotheses are mathematical claims treated separately from this physical adoption. This postulate makes no claim of a hard-sphere Boltzmann–Grad limit, generic gas applicability, spatially inhomogeneous PDE well-posedness, a hydrodynamic limit, or observed entropy increase.

It is not derived from finite-particle mechanics, a hard-sphere Boltzmann–Grad limit, or a general hydrodynamic limit.

items.title: Regularity and invariance of the cutoff Gaussian-mixture class
items.statement:
Fix $u\in\mathbb R^3$ and positive velocity-squared parameters $0<a<b$ (in a physical interpretation, both have units $(\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}})^2$). Let

$$K_{a,b}:=\{\Sigma\in\mathbb R^{3\times3}:\Sigma=\Sigma^{\mathsf T},\ aI\le\Sigma\le bI\},$$

where the matrix inequalities mean $a|z|^2\le z^{\mathsf T}\Sigma z\le b|z|^2$ for every $z\in\mathbb R^3$. For $\Sigma\in K_{a,b}$, define the normalized Gaussian density

$$\gamma_{\Sigma,u}(v):=(2\pi)^{-3/2}(\det\Sigma)^{-1/2}\exp\!\left(-\tfrac12(v-u)^{\mathsf T}\Sigma^{-1}(v-u)\right).$$

Let $\mathcal M_{u,a,b}$ be the closure in the weighted space $X$ of all finite convex mixtures $\sum_{j=1}^N\alpha_j\gamma_{\Sigma_j,u}$ with $\Sigma_j\in K_{a,b}$, $\alpha_j\ge0$, and $\sum_j\alpha_j=1$. Then:

1. Every $f\in\mathcal M_{u,a,b}$ has a $C^\infty$ representative satisfying

$$ (2\pi b)^{-3/2}e^{-|v-u|^2/(2a)}\le f(v)\le(2\pi a)^{-3/2}e^{-|v-u|^2/(2b)}.$$

For every multi-index $\alpha$, there is a finite constant $C_{\alpha,a,b}$, depending only on $\alpha,a,b$ and not on $f$, such that

$$|\partial^\alpha f(v)|\le C_{\alpha,a,b}(1+|v-u|^{|\alpha|})e^{-|v-u|^2/(2b)}.$$

The common derivative bounds imply that every sequence in $\mathcal M_{u,a,b}$ has a subsequence converging locally uniformly together with all velocity derivatives.

2. The gain in [[def-csm-dk-reflection-collision-gain]] maps this class into itself: $\mathcal G(f,g)\in\mathcal M_{u,a,b}$ whenever $f,g\in\mathcal M_{u,a,b}$.

references.title: David Tong, Kinetic Theory, Part 2
R. Fitzpatrick, Plasma Physics, Boltzmann H-Theorem

items.title: Exact kinetic moment balances and unclosed fluxes
items.statement:
Let $\Omega=\prod_{j=1}^3(\mathbb R/L_j\mathbb Z)$ with $L_j>0$, let $I\subset\mathbb R$ be open, and fix $m>0$. Let $F:\Omega\times\mathbb R^3\times I\to[0,\infty)$ be $C^1$, with $n(r,t)=\int F(r,v,t)\,dv>0$. For every compact $J\subset I$, assume some $C_J<\infty$ and $N>6$ satisfy

$$|F|+|\partial_tF|+|\nabla_rF|+|\nabla_vF|\le C_J(1+|v|)^{-N}\qquad(t\in J).$$

Let $a:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R^3$ be $C^1$ and independent of $v$. Let $Q(r,\cdot,t)$ be measurable with $\int(1+|v|^2)|Q|\,dv<\infty$ and

$$\int Q\,dv=0,\qquad \int vQ\,dv=0,\qquad \int |v|^2Q\,dv=0$$

at every $(r,t)$. Suppose pointwise that

$$\partial_tF+v\cdot\nabla_rF+a\cdot\nabla_vF=Q.$$

Define $\rho,u,\Pi,e,q$ as in [[def-csm-dk-kinetic-macroscopic-fields]]. Then the exact balances are

$$\partial_t\rho+\nabla_r\cdot(\rho u)=0,$$

$$\partial_t(\rho u)+\nabla_r\cdot(\rho u\otimes u+\Pi)=\rho a,$$

$$\partial_t\!\left(\frac12\rho|u|^2+e\right)+\nabla_r\cdot\!\left[\left(\frac12\rho|u|^2+e\right)u+\Pi u+q\right]=\rho a\cdot u,$$

and

$$\partial_te+\nabla_r\cdot(eu+q)+\Pi:\nabla_ru=0.$$

These identities are exact moment equations under the stated generic conservation assumptions on $Q$. They do not supply a constitutive relation for $\Pi$ or $q$, a closure, or a hydrodynamic limit.

In the SI physical interpretation, $t$ is measured in seconds, $a$ is acceleration in $\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$, and $Q$ has the units of $F$ per second.

references.title: David Tong, Kinetic Theory, Part 2
R. Fitzpatrick, Plasma Physics, Boltzmann H-Theorem

items.title: Global finite-energy cutoff collision evolution
items.statement:
Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Fix a reference speed $v_0>0$, a rate $\lambda>0$, and the weighted space $X=L^1(\mathbb R^3,w_0\,dv)$ with $w_0(v)=1+|v|^2/v_0^2$, as in [[def-csm-dk-reflection-collision-gain]]. Let $f_0\in X$ be nonnegative with $\int f_0\,dv=1$, first moment $m_1=\int vf_0(v)\,dv$, and finite second moment $E_2=\int |v|^2f_0(v)\,dv$. Put

$$K:=\{g\in X:g\ge0\text{ a.e.},\ \int g\,dv=1,\ \int vg\,dv=m_1,\ \int|v|^2g\,dv=E_2\}.$$

Then there is a unique $f\in C([0,\infty),K)$, with continuity in the $X$ norm, satisfying

$$f_t=e^{-\lambda t}f_0+\lambda\int_0^t e^{-\lambda(t-s)}\mathcal G(f_s,f_s)\,ds,$$

where the time integral is the norm limit of Riemann sums in $X$. For all $t\ge0$, $f_t\ge0$, $\int f_t\,dv=1$, $\int vf_t\,dv=\int vf_0\,dv$, and $\int |v|^2f_t\,dv=E_2$. If $f_0>0$ almost everywhere, then $f_t\ge e^{-\lambda t}f_0$ almost everywhere.

If in addition $f_0\in\mathcal M_{u,a,b}$ for some $u\in\mathbb R^3$ and $0<a<b$, with $\mathcal M_{u,a,b}$ as in [[lem-csm-dk-gaussian-mixture-regularity]], then each $f_t$ has a positive $C^\infty$ velocity representative with the Gaussian bounds in that lemma; these representatives depend continuously on $t$ locally uniformly in velocity, are $C^1$ in $t$, and satisfy $\partial_t f_t=\lambda(\mathcal G(f_t,f_t)-f_t)$ pointwise.

references.title: David Tong, Kinetic Theory, Part 2
R. Fitzpatrick, Plasma Physics, Boltzmann H-Theorem

items.title: H theorem and Maxwellian equality for the regular cutoff model
items.statement:
Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, $v_0>0$, $\lambda>0$, $u\in\mathbb R^3$, and positive velocity-squared parameters $0<a<b$. Let

$$f_0(v)=\tfrac12\gamma_{aI,u}(v)+\tfrac12\gamma_{bI,u}(v),$$

and let $f_t$ be its global solution from [[thm-csm-dk-global-cutoff-collision-evolution]]. Define the dimensionless one-particle functional

$$H(t):=\int_{\mathbb R^3}f_t(v)\log(v_0^3f_t(v))\,dv.$$

For every $t\ge0$, $H$ is finite and continuously differentiable, and with $A=f_t(v)f_t(w)$ and $B=f_t(v')f_t(w')$,

$$H'(t)=-\frac{\lambda}{4}\int_{\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R^3\times S^2}(B-A)\log(B/A)\,d\mu\le0.$$

The integrand is nonnegative. Equality holds at a time $t$ exactly when $f_t$ is a normalized isotropic Gaussian

$$f_t(v)=(2\pi s^2)^{-3/2}\exp\!\left(-\frac{|v-\bar u|^2}{2s^2}\right)$$

for some $\bar u\in\mathbb R^3$ and $s>0$; every such Gaussian is stationary. The specified initial mixture is not a single Gaussian, so $H'(0)<0$.

references.title: David Tong, Kinetic Theory, Part 2
R. Fitzpatrick, Plasma Physics, Boltzmann H-Theorem

items.title: Conditional one-particle kinetic entropy production
items.statement:
Assume the physical adoption [[post-csm-dk-selected-cutoff-kinetic-model]] with a positive collision rate $\lambda$, particle mass $m>0$, reference speed $v_0>0$, and $k_B>0$. Prepare the normalized one-particle velocity density by

$$f_0(v)=\tfrac12\gamma_{aI,u}(v)+\tfrac12\gamma_{bI,u}(v),\qquad u\in\mathbb R^3,\quad 0<a<b,$$

where $u\in\mathbb R^3$ is a mean velocity measured in $\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$, $a,b$ are covariance variances in $(\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}})^2$, and $\gamma_{\Sigma,u}$ is the normalized Gaussian defined in [[lem-csm-dk-gaussian-mixture-regularity]]. For the resulting global regular model solution $f_t$, define the one-particle reference information entropy

$$S_B(t):=-k_B\int_{\mathbb R^3}f_t(v)\log(v_0^3f_t(v))\,dv.$$

Since $v_0^3f_t(v)$ is dimensionless, $S_B$ has SI units $\mathrm{J\,K^{-1}}$.

Then the model deduction is

$$\frac{dS_B}{dt}=\frac{k_B\lambda}{4}\int_{\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R^3\times S^2}(B-A)\log(B/A)\,d\mu\ge0,$$

where $A=f_t(v)f_t(w)$ and $B=f_t(v')f_t(w')$ use the exact reflection variables of [[post-csm-dk-selected-cutoff-kinetic-model]]. The derivative is strictly positive at $t=0$. Equality at any time holds exactly when, for some mean velocity $\bar u\in\mathbb R^3$ and speed parameter $s>0$ (in $\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$),

$$f_t(v)=(2\pi s^2)^{-3/2}\exp\!\left(-\frac{|v-\bar u|^2}{2s^2}\right).$$

This conclusion is conditional on the adopted closed homogeneous model and regular preparation. It identifies a one-particle information functional with entropy units; it does not assert the fine-grained entropy of an $N$-particle ensemble, a general thermodynamic second law, or empirical entropy increase.

references.title: David Tong, Kinetic Theory, Part 2
R. Fitzpatrick, Plasma Physics, Boltzmann H-Theorem

It is not a statement about fine-grained N-particle Gibbs entropy, generic gases, a hard-sphere Boltzmann–Grad limit, hydrodynamic limits, experiments, or all physical realizations.

items.title: Finite reversible stochastic rate model
items.design_state: Complete draft carrier authored; scoped checks and independent review remain pending.
items.statement:
Assume the Axiom of Choice [[def-axiom-of-choice]]. A **finite reversible stochastic rate model** consists of an integer $r\ge2$, the finite state set $E=\{1,\ldots,r\}$, real energy parameters $e_a\in\mathbb R$, an inverse-energy parameter $\beta>0$, and finite transition rates $w_{ab}\ge0$ for distinct $a,b\in E$. When physical units are assigned, $e_a$ is measured in joules, $\beta$ in joules$^{-1}$, and $w_{ab}$ in seconds$^{-1}$; this mathematical definition does not assert a physical realization. Define

$$Z:=\sum_{a\in E}e^{-\beta e_a},\qquad \pi_a:=Z^{-1}e^{-\beta e_a}.$$

Then $Z$ is finite and positive, and $\pi$ is a strictly positive probability vector. Require $w_{ab}>0$ exactly when $w_{ba}>0$, require the undirected graph with edge $\{a,b\}$ whenever $w_{ab}>0$ to be connected, and impose detailed balance $\pi_aw_{ab}=\pi_bw_{ba}$. Define the row generator $Q$ by $Q_{ab}=w_{ab}$ for $a\ne b$ and $Q_{aa}=-q_a$, where $q_a:=\sum_{b\ne a}w_{ab}$. Since $r\ge2$ and the graph is connected, every $q_a>0$. Thus $(Qf)_a=\sum_{b\ne a}w_{ab}(f_b-f_a)$ for a column observable $f$, and a row probability vector evolves by $p'=pQ$.

For any observable $f:E\to\mathbb R$, write $\pi(f):=\sum_{a\in E}\pi_af_a$. For $f,g:E\to\mathbb R$, define $\langle f,g\rangle_\pi:=\sum_{a\in E}\pi_af_ag_a$. Since $E$ is finite and every $\pi_a>0$, all real functions on $E$ belong to this finite-dimensional real inner-product space, denoted $L^2(E,\pi)$; equality in it is pointwise equality.

The associated jump-chain construction waits an exponential time of rate $q_a$ in state $a$ and then selects state $b\ne a$ with probability $w_{ab}/q_a$, using fresh independent random choices at successive jumps. Here an exponential time of rate $q>0$ has survival probability $\Pr(\tau>t)=e^{-qt}$ for $t\ge0$. The Ionescu–Tulcea construction [[thm-ionescu-tulcea-construction-of-a-markov-chain]] supplies the countable random sequence under the stated Choice assumption. The theorem on this page proves nonexplosion, identifies the transition semigroup, and establishes the positive reversible spectral gap. This is a finite mathematical rate model, not a derivation of rates from Hamiltonian mechanics.

items.title: Adopted inertial velocity Langevin bath
items.design_state: Complete draft carrier authored; scoped checks and independent review remain pending.
items.statement:
Assume the Axiom of Choice [[def-axiom-of-choice]], the filtered Brownian probability-space convention of [[def-tdmath-ornstein-uhlenbeck-equation]], and the adopted Newtonian spacetime and frame assumptions of [[post-cm01-frames]]. Fix one inertial frame $\Gamma=(o,u,(e_1,e_2,e_3))$ of that postulate: it is a fixed global adapted affine chart, with $o\in A$, $u\in V$, $\tau(u)=1$, and a fixed positively oriented $g$-orthonormal basis $(e_1,e_2,e_3)$ of the spatial displacement space $K=\ker\tau$. Its chart map assigns each event $p\in A$ the unique coordinates $(t_\Gamma(p),\mathbf x_\Gamma(p))$ satisfying $p=o+t_\Gamma(p)u+\sum_{i=1}^3x_{\Gamma,i}(p)e_i$. Let $X=(X_t)_{t\ge0}$ be the scalar position-coordinate process in this chart, measured in metres, whose value is the signed first spatial coordinate along the fixed axis $e_1$. The model tracks only $X$; it does not specify a full particle worldline or assert a law for either of the other spatial coordinates. Let $X_0$ be an $\mathcal F_0$-measurable real-valued random variable. On a measurable event $\Omega_*\in\mathcal F$ with $P(\Omega_*)=1$, assume $t\mapsto X_t(\omega)$ is continuously differentiable and define the velocity coordinate $V_t(\omega):=dX_t(\omega)/dt$ there, measured in metres per second. Thus $X_t=X_0+\int_0^tV_s\,ds$ on $\Omega_*$; values on the null complement do not affect the stochastic conclusions.

Take a primitive particle mass $m>0$ in kilograms, a primitive constant bath temperature $T_b>0$ in kelvins, and the primitive SI Boltzmann constant $k_B>0$ in joules per kelvin. The positive damping rate $\gamma$ is a primitive model parameter in seconds$^{-1}$; the positive noise amplitude $\sigma$ is derived as the square root of $2\gamma k_BT_b/m$ and has units metres seconds$^{-3/2}$. Let $B_t$ be standard scalar Brownian motion with $B_0=0$, variance $t$ in seconds, and future increments independent of the present filtration. Prepare an $\mathcal F_0$-measurable $V_0\sim N(0,k_BT_b/m)$ independently of future Brownian increments. The force $F:[0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ is a prescribed deterministic locally continuous input in newtons. Adopt

$$V_t=V_0-\gamma\int_0^tV_s\,ds+\frac1m\int_0^tF(s)\,ds+\sigma B_t,\qquad \sigma^2=\frac{2\gamma k_BT_b}{m}.$$

The displayed integral equation is the definition of the stochastic differential notation $dV_t=-\gamma V_t\,dt+F(t)\,dt/m+\sigma\,dB_t$. Brownian increments have units seconds$^{1/2}$, so every term in the equation for $V_t$ has units metres seconds$^{-1}$. When $F=0$, the preparation is the stationary OU Gaussian law because its variance is $\sigma^2/(2\gamma)=k_BT_b/m$; the cited mathematical supplier establishes the specified OU model properties. The thermal noise normalization, Gaussian preparation, constant damping, and deterministic force coupling are adopted assumptions. No measurement, material calibration, nonlinear response, or microscopic derivation of this bath is asserted.

items.title: Adopted finite reversible bath rates and field coupling
items.design_state: Complete draft carrier authored; scoped checks and independent review remain pending.
items.statement:
Use the finite state set, energies $e_a$, rates $w_{ab}$, Gibbs weights $\pi_a$, and row generator $Q$ defined in [[def-csm-dk-finite-reversible-rate-model]]. Assign the state energies the physical meaning of coarse-state energies in joules. Use the primitive SI Boltzmann constant $k_B$ in joules per kelvin from [[post-csm-dk-selected-thermal-langevin-bath]], and set $\beta=(k_BT_b)^{-1}$ in joules$^{-1}$ for the positive bath-temperature parameter $T_b$ in kelvins. Adopt the baseline transition rates $w_{ab}$ in seconds$^{-1}$ and the initial law $p_0=\pi$ for the equilibrium-response branch. These choices define a finite phenomenological thermal rate model; they do not say that a real material has these rates.

Fix a finite time horizon $t_f>0$. For a fixed state observable $B:E\to\mathbb R$ with units denoted $[B]$, a dimensionless control amplitude $\epsilon$, and a continuous field $h:[0,t_f]\to\mathbb R$ with units joules per $[B]$, adopt the controlled rates

$$w_{ab}^{\epsilon}(t)=w_{ab}\exp\!\left(\frac{\beta\epsilon h(t)}2(B_b-B_a)\right),\qquad a\ne b.$$

Their units remain seconds$^{-1}$ because the exponent is dimensionless. This is one explicit symmetric allocation of the field-dependent rate factor. For constant $h$ and each positive-rate edge ($w_{ab}>0$, equivalently $w_{ba}>0$), the rate ratio obeys

$$\frac{w_{ab}^{\epsilon}}{w_{ba}^{\epsilon}}=\exp\!\left(-\beta\left[(e_b-\epsilon hB_b)-(e_a-\epsilon hB_a)\right]\right),$$

so the Gibbs weights of the shifted energies $e_a-\epsilon hB_a$ satisfy detailed balance by direct multiplication on every positive-rate edge. For an absent edge, both controlled rates remain zero, so the detailed-balance product identity holds there as well; no rate ratio is defined there. A rate ratio alone leaves state-pair prefactors undetermined; the symmetric splitting above is an additional modeling choice and is the specific perturbation analyzed in the consuming theorem. No experiment or empirical rate estimate is asserted.

items.title: Nonexplosive finite continuous-time chain and reversible spectral gap
items.design_state: Complete draft carrier authored; scoped checks and independent review remain pending.
items.statement:
Assume the Axiom of Choice [[def-axiom-of-choice]] and let $E,\pi,w,Q$ be the finite model data of [[def-csm-dk-finite-reversible-rate-model]], with $|E|=r\ge2$. For every initial probability row vector $p_0$, there exists a time-homogeneous continuous-time Markov chain $X_t$ on $E$, $t\ge0$, with no finite accumulation of jumps, transition matrix $P_t=e^{tQ}$, and law $p_t=p_0P_t$. The detailed-balance law $\pi$ is stationary. On the real inner-product space $L^2(E,\pi)$, $Q$ is self-adjoint and has an orthonormal eigenbasis $\phi_0=1,\phi_1,\ldots,\phi_{r-1}$ with eigenvalues $0,-\lambda_1,\ldots,-\lambda_{r-1}$, where every $\lambda_j>0$. Thus the spectral gap $\lambda_*:=\min_j\lambda_j$ is positive and $P_t$ converges exponentially to projection onto constants.

Here a finite-state continuous-time Markov chain means a process with piecewise-constant paths whose conditional transition matrix over an interval of length $t$ is $P_t$, independent of the starting time. For initial law $\pi$, the chain has a two-sided stationary extension $X_t$, $t\in\mathbb R$, whose finite-dimensional laws at $t_1<\cdots<t_n$ are $\pi_{a_1}\prod_{i=1}^{n-1}P_{t_{i+1}-t_i}(a_i,a_{i+1})$. Its sample paths are locally piecewise constant with finitely many jumps on every bounded time interval.

items.title: Exact OU velocity response, diffusion and Gaussian scaling
items.design_state: Complete draft carrier authored; scoped checks and independent review remain pending.
items.statement:
Assume the Axiom of Choice [[def-axiom-of-choice]] and the Brownian probability-space hypotheses in [[def-tdmath-ornstein-uhlenbeck-equation]]. Let $\gamma,m,\Theta,k_B>0$, $\sigma>0$, and $\sigma^2=2\gamma k_B\Theta/m$. Here these are real mathematical parameters; a separate physics postulate assigns their physical units and interpretation. Let $V_0:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ be $\mathcal F_0$-measurable, satisfy $V_0\sim N(0,k_B\Theta/m)$ and be independent of future Brownian increments. For any locally continuous deterministic input $u:[0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$, and every finite $t_f>0$, the equation restricted to $[0,t_f]$
$$V_t=V_0-\gamma\int_0^tV_s\,ds+\frac1m\int_0^tu(s)\,ds+\sigma B_t,\qquad 0\le t\le t_f,$$
has a unique continuous solution; these unique finite-horizon solutions agree on overlapping intervals and define one solution for all $t\ge0$. Its mean is
$$\mathbb E V_t=\frac1m\int_0^te^{-\gamma(t-s)}u(s)\,ds.$$
For $u=0$, $V$ is a stationary centered Gaussian process on $[0,\infty)$ with covariance
$$\mathbb E[V_sV_t]=v_\Theta e^{-\gamma|t-s|},\qquad v_\Theta:=k_B\Theta/m.$$
Define $Y_t:=\int_0^tV_s\,ds$ and $D:=v_\Theta/\gamma$. Then
$$\operatorname{Var}(Y_t)=2v_\Theta\left(\frac{t}{\gamma}-\frac{1-e^{-\gamma t}}{\gamma^2}\right),\qquad \lim_{t\to\infty}\frac{\operatorname{Var}(Y_t)}{2t}=D.$$
For every deterministic input, the centered displacement $Y_t-\mathbb E Y_t$ is Gaussian with the variance above; consequently $(Y_t-\mathbb E Y_t)/\sqrt t$ converges in distribution to $N(0,2D)$. For constant input $u(s)=u_0$, $\lim_{t\to\infty}\mathbb E[V_t]/u_0=\chi:=1/(m\gamma)$ when $u_0\ne0$, and $D=\chi k_B\Theta$.

items.title: Conditional Langevin Green–Kubo and Einstein relation
items.design_state: Complete draft carrier authored; scoped checks and independent review remain pending.
items.statement:
Assume the adopted velocity bath [[post-csm-dk-selected-thermal-langevin-bath]] on $t\ge0$ and the Axiom of Choice [[def-axiom-of-choice]]. Let $X_t=X_0+\int_0^tV_s\,ds$ be the position coordinate in that model, and prepare $V_0$ in its specified stationary Gaussian law. For zero external force, define the stationary velocity covariance by
$$C_{VV}(\tau):=\mathbb E[(V_s-\mathbb EV_s)(V_{s+\tau}-\mathbb EV_{s+\tau})],\qquad s\ge\max(0,-\tau).$$
Stationarity makes it independent of $s$, and the model gives
$$C_{VV}(\tau)=\frac{k_BT_b}{m}e^{-\gamma|\tau|}.$$
For a deterministic force applied at time $s\le t$, the linear response kernel is
$$R_{VF}(t-s)=\frac1m e^{-\gamma(t-s)}=\frac{1}{k_BT_b}C_{VV}(t-s).$$
Here $R_{VF}$ is defined by the exact mean-response formula
$$\mathbb E[V_t]=\int_0^tR_{VF}(t-s)F(s)\,ds$$
for deterministic forcing from the stated zero-mean stationary preparation; its units are $\mathrm{kg^{-1}}$. The constant-force mobility below is a distinct steady-response coefficient.
The diffusion coefficient defined by centered displacement variance satisfies the Green–Kubo identity
$$D:=\lim_{t\to\infty}\frac{\operatorname{Var}(X_t-X_0)}{2t}=\frac{k_BT_b}{m\gamma}\quad\text{in }\mathrm{m^2\,s^{-1}}.$$
More precisely, $D=\int_0^\infty C_{VV}(\tau)\,d\tau$.
The constant-force mobility
$$\mu:=\lim_{t\to\infty}\frac{\mathbb E[V_t]}{F_0}=\frac1{m\gamma}\quad\text{in }\mathrm{s\,kg^{-1}}$$
for constant $F_0\ne0$. Hence $D=\mu k_BT_b$. The centered displacement divided by $\sqrt t$ converges in distribution to $N(0,2D)$. These are conditional model deductions, not observed transport data or a universal law for arbitrary systems.

items.title: Finite-rate fluctuation response and Green–Kubo inverse
items.design_state: Complete draft carrier authored; scoped checks and independent review remain pending.
items.statement:
Assume the Axiom of Choice [[def-axiom-of-choice]], countable choice [[def-countable-choice]], and the rate model $E,\pi,w,Q$ of [[def-csm-dk-finite-reversible-rate-model]]. Let $X_t$ be the stationary two-sided chain of [[thm-csm-dk-nonexplosive-ctmc-and-gap]], with transition semigroup $P_t=e^{tQ}$. For any real observables $A,B:E\to\mathbb R$, write $A_c=A-\pi(A)$ and $B_c=B-\pi(B)$, and define
$$C_{BA}(t):=\langle B_c,P_tA_c\rangle_\pi,\qquad t\ge0.$$
Define $\operatorname{Cov}_\pi(A,B):=\pi(AB)-\pi(A)\pi(B)$, where $AB$ is pointwise multiplication.
For any finite horizon $t_f>0$, let $h:[0,t_f]\to\mathbb R$ be continuous and let $\epsilon$ be dimensionless. For $0\le t\le t_f$, prescribe rates
$$w^\epsilon_{ab}(t)=w_{ab}\exp\! \left(\frac{\beta\epsilon h(t)}2(B_b-B_a)\right),\quad a\ne b,$$
with negative row sums on the diagonal, and let $p^\epsilon(0)=\pi$ evolve by the resulting finite forward equation. For $0\le t\le t_f$, the derivative of the observable mean at $\epsilon=0$ is
$$\left.\frac{\partial}{\partial\epsilon}\sum_a p^\epsilon_a(t)A_a\right|_{\epsilon=0}=\int_0^t h(s)R_{AB}(t-s)\,ds,\qquad R_{AB}(u)=-\beta\,\frac{d}{du}C_{BA}(u).$$
For a constant field $h$, define the normalized perturbed Gibbs vector by
$$\pi^\epsilon_a:=\frac{\pi_a e^{\beta\epsilon hB_a}}{\sum_{c\in E}\pi_c e^{\beta\epsilon hB_c}}.$$
It is stationary and its static susceptibility is $\beta h\,\operatorname{Cov}_\pi(A,B)$.

For any bounded vector observable $G:E\to\mathbb R^d$, set $G_c=G-\pi(G)$ and
$$C_{ij}(s):=\langle (G_c)_i,P_s(G_c)_j\rangle_\pi.$$
These correlations are absolutely integrable. The Green–Kubo covariance limit is
$$\lim_{T\to\infty}\frac{\operatorname{Cov}_\pi(\int_0^T G(X_s)\,ds)}{2T}=D,\qquad D_{ij}=\int_0^\infty C_{ij}(s)\,ds=\langle (G_c)_i,(-Q)^{-1}(G_c)_j\rangle_\pi,$$
where $(-Q)^{-1}$ is the inverse on the mean-zero subspace and $D$ is positive semidefinite.

items.title: Markov relative entropy decay and almost-sure time averages
items.design_state: Complete draft carrier authored; scoped checks and independent review remain pending.
items.statement:
Assume the Axiom of Choice [[def-axiom-of-choice]], countable choice [[def-countable-choice]], and the model $E,\pi,w,Q$ of [[def-csm-dk-finite-reversible-rate-model]]. For any initial probability vector $p_0$, let $p_t=p_0P_t$, where $P_t=e^{tQ}$ is supplied by [[thm-csm-dk-nonexplosive-ctmc-and-gap]], and define the dimensionless relative information
$$\mathcal D(p_t\Vert\pi):=\sum_{a\in E}p_a(t)\log\frac{p_a(t)}{\pi_a},\qquad 0\log0:=0.$$
For every $t>0$, $p_a(t)>0$ for all states and
$$\frac{d}{dt}\mathcal D(p_t\Vert\pi)=-\frac12\sum_{a\in E}\sum_{b\ne a}\pi_aw_{ab}(r_b(t)-r_a(t))(\log r_b(t)-\log r_a(t))\le0,\qquad r_a(t):=\frac{p_a(t)}{\pi_a}.$$
At a positive time the derivative vanishes exactly when $p_t=\pi$, and $\mathcal D(p_t\Vert\pi)\to0$ as $t\to\infty$.

For every bounded observable $A:E\to\mathbb R$ and every initial law, the actual continuous-time average satisfies
$$\frac1T\int_0^T A(X_s)\,ds\longrightarrow\pi(A)\quad\text{almost surely as }T\to\infty.$$
Under stationary preparation, with $A_c=A-\pi(A)$ and spectral gap $\lambda_*$ from [[thm-csm-dk-nonexplosive-ctmc-and-gap]],
$$\operatorname{Var}_\pi\!\left(\frac1T\int_0^T A(X_s)\,ds\right)\le\frac{2\|A_c\|_{L^2(\pi)}^2}{\lambda_*T}.$$

items.title: Exact all-preparations coarse Markov criterion
items.design_state: Complete draft carrier authored; scoped checks and independent review remain pending.
items.statement:
Assume the Axiom of Choice [[def-axiom-of-choice]] and the finite rate chain of [[def-csm-dk-finite-reversible-rate-model]] with transition semigroup supplied by [[thm-csm-dk-nonexplosive-ctmc-and-gap]]. Let $\mathcal C=\{C_1,\ldots,C_k\}$ be a partition of $E$, meaning $k\ge1$, each $C_i$ is nonempty, the blocks are pairwise disjoint, and their union is $E$. For $a\in C_i$ and $j
e i$, set
$$q(a,C_j):=\sum_{b\in C_j}w_{ab}.$$
The projected process $ ar X_t=i$ when $X_t\in C_i$ has one time-homogeneous Markov generator valid for every initial microscopic probability law if and only if $q(a,C_j)$ is independent of $a\in C_i$ for every $i$ and $j
e i$. Under this condition, the coarse generator has off-diagonal entries $ ar q_{ij}=q(a,C_j)$ for any $a\in C_i$ and diagonal entries $ ar q_{ii}=-\sum_{j
e i} ar q_{ij}$. Its stationary weights $ ar\pi_i=\sum_{a\in C_i}\pi_a$ satisfy detailed balance.

items.title: Conditional finite-state equilibration and fluctuation response
items.design_state: Complete draft carrier authored; scoped checks and independent review remain pending.
items.statement:
Assume the adopted finite thermal rate model [[post-csm-dk-selected-reversible-bath-rates]], including its finite energy states, detailed-balance rates, temperature parameter and stationary Gibbs preparation for the response branch. For any initial microscopic probability law, the model's dimensionless relative information $\mathcal D(p_t\Vert\pi)$ is nonincreasing and tends to zero, and every bounded state observable has an almost-sure time average equal to its Gibbs mean. For real state observables $A,B:E\to\mathbb R$, any finite horizon $t_f>0$, and a continuous field $h:[0,t_f]\to\mathbb R$, the equilibrium-response branch with the postulated symmetric field-dependent rates has, for $0\le t\le t_f$, first-order response
$$\delta\langle A(t)\rangle=\int_0^t h(s)\left[-\beta\,\frac{d}{du}C_{BA}(u)\bigg|_{u=t-s}\right]ds,$$
where $\delta\langle A(t)\rangle:=\left.\partial_\epsilon\sum_a p_a^\epsilon(t)A_a\right|_{\epsilon=0}$, $p^\epsilon(0)=\pi$, and $p^\epsilon$ solves the finite forward equation for the postulated controlled rates. The correlation is $C_{BA}(u)=\langle(B-\pi(B)),P_u(A-\pi(A))\rangle_\pi$. For a constant field amplitude $g$ (in joules per unit of $B$), define the normalized perturbed equilibrium vector by $\pi^g_a:=\frac{\pi_a e^{\beta gB_a}}{\sum_{c\in E}\pi_c e^{\beta gB_c}}$ and define its susceptibility per unit field by $\chi_{AB}:=\left.\partial_g\pi^g(A)\right|_{g=0}$. Then $\chi_{AB}=\beta\,\operatorname{Cov}_\pi(A,B)$ and, when $g=\epsilon h$ for constant $h$, the derivative with respect to dimensionless $\epsilon$ is $h\chi_{AB}$. Here $\pi^g(A):=\sum_a\pi^g_aA_a$ and $\operatorname{Cov}_\pi(A,B):=\pi(AB)-\pi(A)\pi(B)$. If physical units are assigned to $A$ and $B$, write them as $[A]$ and $[B]$: $C_{BA}$ has units $[A][B]$, while $\beta h\,dC_{BA}/du$ has units $[A]$ per second, so the time integral and the derivative with respect to dimensionless $\epsilon$ have units $[A]$. These are conditional predictions of this finite stochastic model. They concern its dimensionless relative-information functional and state observables; no experimental observation, calibrated rate, material-specific claim or universal thermodynamic law is asserted.

items.title: Gaussian, gamma and beta product integrals
items.design_state: Initial authoring complete; current prerequisite availability and readiness disposition are recorded in batch evidence.
items.statement:
For $a>0$ and an integer $r\ge0$, define $I_r(a):=\int_{\mathbb R}x^{2r}e^{-ax^2}\,dx$ as the two-sided improper Riemann integral. Then

$$I_r(a)=\frac{\Gamma(r+\tfrac12)}{a^{r+1/2}},\qquad \int_{\mathbb R}x^{2r+1}e^{-ax^2}\,dx=0,$$

where $\Gamma(s):=\int_0^\infty t^{s-1}e^{-t}\,dt$ for $s>0$. In particular, $I_0(a)=\sqrt{\pi/a}$ and $I_1(a)=\sqrt\pi/(2a^{3/2})$. For every compact interval $K=[a_0,a_1]\subset(0,\infty)$, $I_r$ is continuously differentiable on $K$ and

$$I_r'(a)=-I_{r+1}(a).$$

For $s,t>0$, put $B(s,t):=\int_0^1u^{s-1}(1-u)^{t-1}\,du$. Then $B(s,t)$ is finite and

$$\Gamma(s)\Gamma(t)=\Gamma(s+t)B(s,t),\qquad \Gamma(s+1)=s\Gamma(s),\qquad \Gamma(\tfrac12)=\sqrt\pi.$$

Consequently, if independent positive random variables have densities $x^{s-1}e^{-x}/\Gamma(s)$ and $x^{t-1}e^{-x}/\Gamma(t)$, their sum has density $x^{s+t-1}e^{-x}/\Gamma(s+t)$.
items.strategy:
1.1 For $s>0$, the gamma integrand on $(0,1)$ is bounded by $t^{s-1}$, whose integral is $1/s$. For $t\ge1$, $t^{s-1}e^{-t/2}$ is bounded, so $t^{s-1}e^{-t}\le C_se^{-t/2}$ and the tail converges. On a compact positive $s$-interval, the lower endpoint bounds the near-zero power and the upper endpoint bounds the exponential tail uniformly. Hence $\Gamma(s)$ is finite and has controlled endpoint tails. [given, algebra]

1.2 Let $I=\int_{\mathbb R}e^{-x^2}dx$. By [F2], $I^2$ equals the nonnegative plane Gaussian integral, and [F3] evaluates that integral as $\pi$. Hence $I^2=\pi$. [F2, F3, algebra]

2.1 By [F1], $I$ is finite and positive. The positive square root in step 1.2 is therefore $I=\sqrt\pi$. [F1, step 1.2, algebra]

2.2 Integration by parts on $[\varepsilon,R]$ gives $\int_\varepsilon^R t^se^{-t}\,dt=[-t^se^{-t}]_\varepsilon^R+s\int_\varepsilon^R t^{s-1}e^{-t}\,dt$. The boundary terms vanish by step 1.1, so $\Gamma(s+1)=s\Gamma(s)$; direct integration gives $\Gamma(1)=1$. [step 1.1, algebra]

2.3 For $s,t>0$, the beta integrand is integrable near $0$ by comparison with $u^{s-1}$ and near $1$ by comparison with $(1-u)^{t-1}$. On each compact rectangle $[1/j,j]^2$ the continuous product integrand $x^{s-1}y^{t-1}e^{-(x+y)}$ has integral equal to the product of its one-dimensional integrals, as follows by factoring the finite rectangular Riemann sums. These nested rectangles exhaust the positive quadrant and their integrals tend to $\Gamma(s)\Gamma(t)$ by step 1.1. [step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 Substitution $t=x^2$ on compact half-intervals and passage to the convergent improper limits gives $\Gamma(\tfrac12)=2\int_0^\infty e^{-x^2}\,dx=I=\sqrt\pi$ by steps 1.2 and 2.1. [step 1.2, step 2.1, algebra]

3.2 On $A_j=[1/j,j]\times[1/j,1-1/j]$ in coordinates $(r,u)$, the map $\Phi(r,u)=(ru,r(1-u))$ is injective, has determinant $-r\ne0$, and is a $C^1$ diffeomorphism on an open neighborhood. Its image is a compact Jordan set. The images exhaust the positive quadrant cofinally with the rectangles in step 2.3: each compact rectangle stays a positive distance from both axes and has bounded $x+y$, while each image is compact and stays away from the axes. Applying [F4] on $A_j$ and taking the increasing limits gives $\Gamma(s)\Gamma(t)=\int_0^\infty r^{s+t-1}e^{-r}\,dr\,B(s,t)=\Gamma(s+t)B(s,t)$. The limits are finite by step 1.1 and the endpoint bounds in step 2.3. [step 1.1, step 2.3, F4, algebra]

4.1 For integer $r\ge0$, $x^{2r}e^{-ax^2/2}$ is bounded on $\mathbb R$, so $x^{2r}e^{-ax^2}\le C e^{-ax^2/2}$ and [F1] gives absolute convergence; odd moments converge absolutely and vanish by reflection. On compact intervals the substitution $y=\sqrt a\,x$ is covered by [F4], and its improper limit gives $I_0(a)=a^{-1/2}I_0(1)=\sqrt{\pi/a}$ by steps 1.2 and 2.1. The substitution $t=ax^2$ on both half-lines gives $I_r(a)=a^{-r-1/2}\Gamma(r+\tfrac12)$; finiteness follows from step 1.1, the half-integer starting value from step 3.1, and recurrence from step 2.2. [given, F1, F4, step 1.1, step 1.2, step 2.1, step 2.2, step 3.1, algebra]

5.1 Fix the integer $r\ge0$. Step 4.1 evaluated $I_r(a)=\Gamma(r+\tfrac12)a^{-r-1/2}$ for every $a>0$ using only convergent improper substitutions, and step 2.2 proved the Gamma recurrence by integration by parts; neither argument used parameter differentiation. By [F5], differentiation of this established explicit function gives $$I_r'(a)=-(r+\tfrac12)\Gamma(r+\tfrac12)a^{-r-3/2}=-\Gamma(r+\tfrac32)a^{-r-3/2}=-I_{r+1}(a).$$ The same positive-base power formula makes this derivative continuous on $(0,\infty)$, hence on a neighborhood of every compact $K\subset(0,\infty)$. This proves the full parameter clause without interchanging a derivative and an improper integral. [F5, step 2.2, step 4.1, algebra]

6.1 Let $C=[c,d]\subset(0,\infty)$ and set $Q_j=[1/j,j]^2$. The event $A_j=Q_j\cap\{(x,y):x+y\in C\}$ is Jordan measurable. On each grid rectangle $I\times J\subset Q_j$, independence gives probability $P(X\in I)P(Y\in J)=(\int_I f_s)(\int_J f_t)$; because the marginal densities are continuous on $Q_j$, the finite rectangular Riemann sums factor and converge to the integral of $f_s(x)f_t(y)$ on that rectangle. The inner and outer grid unions for $A_j$ differ only in cells meeting its finitely many line-segment boundary pieces; their total area tends to zero, and $f_sf_t$ is bounded on $Q_j$. Thus $P((X,Y)\in A_j)=\int_{A_j}f_sf_t\,dx\,dy$. As $Q_j$ increases to the positive quadrant, countable additivity gives probabilities increasing to $P(X+Y\in C)$, and the nonnegative improper integrals increase to the integral over $x,y>0$. The images of $C\times[1/j,1-1/j]$ under $(r,u)\mapsto(ru,r(1-u))$ increase to $A_C=\{x,y>0:x+y\in C\}$. On each such compact set the map is injective with absolute Jacobian $r$, so [F4] transforms the integral to $r^{s+t-1}e^{-r}u^{s-1}(1-u)^{t-1}/(\Gamma(s)\Gamma(t))$. Its rectangular Riemann sums factor; as $j\to\infty$ the $u$-integral tends to $B(s,t)$. By step 3.2, $P(X+Y\in C)=\int_C r^{s+t-1}e^{-r}/\Gamma(s+t)\,dr$. A singleton C has probability zero by the same zero-area grid-boundary argument. The density integrates to one by step 1.1, so these interval probabilities determine the sum law. [given, step 1.1, step 3.2, F4, algebra] ∎

references.title: Michael E. Taylor, Introduction to Analysis in Several Variables (Advanced Calculus), §3.1, equations (3.1.72)–(3.1.75)
NIST Digital Library of Mathematical Functions, §5.2(i), Euler's integral

items.title: Jacobian identity for a specified smooth diffeomorphic flow
items.design_state: Initial authoring complete; current prerequisite availability and readiness disposition are recorded in batch evidence.
items.statement:
Let $n\ge1$, let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an open interval containing $0$, and let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open. Suppose $\chi:I\times U\to\mathbb R^n$ is jointly $C^2$, each $\chi_t(a):=\chi(t,a)$ is a $C^2$ diffeomorphism from $U$ onto an open set $U_t$, and $\chi_0(a)=a$. Let $D:=\{(t,x):t\in I,\ x\in U_t\}$ be open and let $b:D\to\mathbb R^n$ be $C^1$ with $\partial_t\chi(t,a)=b(t,\chi(t,a))$. Define $F(t,a):=D_a\chi(t,a)$, $J(t,a):=\det F(t,a)$, and $\operatorname{div}b:=\sum_{i=1}^n\partial_{x_i}b_i$. Then

$$\partial_tF=(D_xb)(t,\chi)F,\qquad \partial_tJ=J(\operatorname{div}b)(t,\chi),\qquad J(0,a)=1.$$

In particular $J(t,a)>0$ for all $(t,a)\in I\times U$, and if $\operatorname{div}b=0$ on $D$, then $J(t,a)=1$. The same identities hold on the flat torus $\mathbb T^n:=\mathbb R^n/\Lambda$, where $\Lambda=\mathbb Z\ell_1+\cdots+\mathbb Z\ell_n$ for a linearly independent basis $\ell_1,\ldots,\ell_n$ and the smooth structure and Euclidean metric descend from $\mathbb R^n$. In that clause, let $\chi:I\times\mathbb T^n\to\mathbb T^n$ be jointly $C^2$, with each $\chi_t$ a diffeomorphism and $\chi_0=\operatorname{id}$. Let $\pi:T\mathbb T^n\to\mathbb T^n$ be the tangent-bundle projection, and let $b:I\times\mathbb T^n\to T\mathbb T^n$ have $C^1$ chart coefficients and satisfy $\pi(b(t,a))=a$ and $\partial_t\chi(t,a)=b(t,\chi(t,a))$. In every translation chart write $b=\sum_i b^i\partial_{x^i}$ and define $\operatorname{div}b:=\sum_i\partial_{x^i}b^i$. Define $F(t,a)$ to be the matrix of $D_a\chi_t:T_a\mathbb T^n\to T_{\chi_t(a)}\mathbb T^n$ in the translation frames and $J(t,a):=\det F(t,a)$. Translation-chart changes have derivative $I$, so these matrices, determinants and divergences agree on overlaps. These are identities for supplied flow data; no existence or global-flow theorem is asserted.
items.strategy:
1.1 For each component $\chi_i$, joint $C^2$ regularity and [F1] give $\partial_t\partial_{a_j}\chi_i=\partial_{a_j}\partial_t\chi_i$. Differentiating the given velocity equation in $a$ and applying [F2] yields $\partial_tF=LF$, where $L(t,a):=(D_xb)(t,\chi(t,a))$. [given, F1, F2, algebra]

2.1 Each $F(t,a)$ is invertible: differentiating $\chi_t^{-1}\circ\chi_t=\operatorname{id}$ by [F2] gives $D\chi_t^{-1}(\chi_t(a))F(t,a)=I$. Thus [F3] applies to the $C^1$ matrix curve $t\mapsto F(t,a)$ and gives $\partial_tJ=J\operatorname{tr}(F^{-1}LF)$. [given, F2, F3, step 1.1]

3.1 By [F4], $\operatorname{tr}(F^{-1}LF)=\operatorname{tr}(FF^{-1}L)=\operatorname{tr}L=\sum_i\partial_{x_i}b_i(t,\chi(t,a))$. Also $F(0,a)=I$, so $J(0,a)=1$. [F4, step 1.1, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 The determinant $J(t,a)$ is continuous and nonzero on $I$ by step 2.1. If it were negative for some $t$, [F6] on the closed segment with endpoints $0$ and $t$ would give a point where $J=0$, contradicting invertibility. Hence $J>0$. [given, F6, step 2.1, step 3.1]

4.2 If $\operatorname{div}b=0$, step 3.1 gives $\partial_tJ=0$. For each fixed $a$, the case $t=0$ is already $J(0,a)=1$. For $t\ne0$, apply [F5] to $J(\cdot,a)$ on $[\min(0,t),\max(0,t)]$, whose endpoints are distinct; since its derivative is zero, its endpoint difference is zero, so $J(t,a)=J(0,a)=1$. [given, F5, step 3.1, algebra]

5.1 For the torus clause, fix $a\in\mathbb T^n$ and $t_0\in I$. By continuity, choose a time neighborhood of $t_0$ on which $a$ and $\chi_t(a)$ stay in translation charts. Their transition maps are translations, so the coordinate matrices of $D_a\chi_t$, their determinants, and the coordinate divergence of $b$ agree on overlaps. In these charts the Euclidean calculations in steps 1.1–3.1 prove both differential identities, and $\chi_0=\operatorname{id}$ gives $J(0,a)=1$. Since $t_0$ was arbitrary, the identities hold throughout $I$; applying steps 4.1 and 4.2 on the closed segment between $0$ and any $t\in I$ gives positivity and the divergence-free conclusion. [given, step 1.1, step 2.1, step 3.1, step 4.1, step 4.2] ∎

references.title: Michael E. Taylor, Introduction to Analysis in Several Variables (Advanced Calculus), §§2.1–2.3
Sheldon Axler, Linear Algebra Done Right, 4th edition, Theorem 8.49

items.title: Fine entropy under a specified incompressible periodic flow
items.design_state: Initial authoring complete; current prerequisite availability and readiness disposition are recorded in batch evidence.
items.statement: Use $\log$ for the natural logarithm of [[def-natural-logarithm]]. Let $\mathbb T^n:=\mathbb R^n/\Lambda$ be a flat translation torus, where $\Lambda=\mathbb Z\ell_1+\cdots+\mathbb Z\ell_n$ for a linearly independent basis $\ell_1,\ldots,\ell_n$, with the smooth structure and Euclidean metric descended from $\mathbb R^n$. Let $\mu=c\,da$ be its fixed translation-invariant volume measure in dimensionless translation coordinates, with $c>0$. Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an open interval containing $0$. Suppose $\chi:I\times\mathbb T^n\to\mathbb T^n$ is jointly $C^2$, each $\chi_t$ is a diffeomorphism, and $\chi_0=\operatorname{id}$. Let $\pi:T\mathbb T^n\to\mathbb T^n$ be the tangent-bundle projection and let $b:I\times\mathbb T^n\to T\mathbb T^n$ have $C^1$ chart coefficients with $\pi(b(t,a))=a$ and $\partial_t\chi(t,a)=b(t,\chi(t,a))$. In translation charts write $b=\sum_i b^i\partial_{x^i}$ and define $\operatorname{div}b=\sum_i\partial_{x^i}b^i$. Assume $\operatorname{div}b=0$ in these charts. Let $f_0\in C^1(\mathbb T^n)$ satisfy $0<m\le f_0\le M<\infty$ and $\int f_0\,d\mu=1$, and define $f_t:=f_0\circ\chi_t^{-1}$. Then $f_t$ is a probability density for every $t\in I$, the integral $H(f_t):=-\int_{\mathbb T^n}f_t\log f_t\,d\mu$ is finite, and $H(f_t)=H(f_0)$. Here $H$ is the dimensionless fine entropy of this density; multiplication by a physical constant such as $k_B$ is a separate interpretation.
items.strategy:
1.1 Apply [F1] to the given family. Its hypotheses are exactly the supplied $C^2$ diffeomorphisms, identity initial map and $C^1$ divergence-free velocity, so every local translation-chart Jacobian is $J_t=1$. [given, F1]



2.1 For fixed $t$, around each point choose a source chart and a smaller coordinate neighborhood whose closure maps under $\chi_t$ into a target chart. Continuity and compactness give finitely many closed coordinate boxes $Q_j$ with interiors covering the torus and with each $\chi_t(Q_j)$ inside a target chart. Put $E_1=Q_1$ and $E_j=Q_j\setminus\bigcup_{i<j}\operatorname{int}(Q_i)$; each $E_j$ is compact, the pieces cover the torus, and any overlap lies on one of the box faces. Each $E_j$ is Jordan because its boundary lies in a finite union of coordinate faces, which are compact $C^1$ hypersurface patches. A $C^1$ graph patch has bounded slope on a compact subpatch, so its mesh-$h$ box cover has total $n$-volume $O(h)$ and hence content zero. On compact chart neighborhoods $\chi_t$ has bounded derivative, so it maps these zero-content boundaries to zero-content boundaries. Each compact piece and its image therefore have Jordan boundaries and lie in source and target charts; [F2] applies there. Summing over the pieces, overlaps do not affect the integrals, translation chart changes preserve $da$, and the constant $c$ is the same on both sides. Thus for every continuous $\varphi$ on the torus, $\int\varphi\circ\chi_t\,d\mu=\int\varphi J_t\,d\mu=\int\varphi\,d\mu$. [given, F1, F2, step 1.1]



3.1 The function $f_t=f_0\circ\chi_t^{-1}$ is positive and continuous. The substitution of step 2.1 with $\varphi=f_t$ gives $\int f_t\,d\mu=\int f_0\,d\mu=1$, so $f_t$ is normalized. [given, step 2.1]



4.1 The bounds $m\le f_0\le M$ also hold for $f_t$; by [F3], $\log$ is continuous on $[m,M]$, so $f_t\log f_t$ is bounded and continuous on the compact torus and its integral is finite. Applying step 2.1 to $\varphi=f_t\log f_t$ gives $\int f_t\log f_t\,d\mu=\int (f_t\log f_t)\circ\chi_t\,d\mu=\int f_0\log f_0\,d\mu$, since $f_t\circ\chi_t=f_0$. Negating proves $H(f_t)=H(f_0)$. [given, F3, step 2.1, algebra] ∎

references.title: Michael E. Taylor, Introduction to Analysis in Several Variables (Advanced Calculus), §3.1 and Chapter 4, §4.5
David Tong, Statistical Physics, §1.2, entropy as a functional of a specified state

items.title: Gaussian covariance for positive quadratic forms and a boundary counterexample
items.design_state: Initial authoring complete; current prerequisite availability and readiness disposition are recorded in batch evidence.
items.statement:
Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ as defined in [[def-countable-choice]]. Let $n\ge1$, let $K\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}$ be symmetric positive definite, and let $\beta>0$. For $x\in\mathbb R^n$ put $H(x)=\tfrac12x^{\mathsf T}Kx$, and use the Euclidean Lebesgue measure $\lambda_n$ to define the density $Z^{-1}e^{-\beta H(x)}$. Then

$$Z=\int_{\mathbb R^n}e^{-\beta H(x)}dx=\left(\frac{2\pi}{\beta}\right)^{n/2}(\det K)^{-1/2},\quad \mathbb E[x]=0,\quad \mathbb E[xx^{\mathsf T}]=\beta^{-1}K^{-1},\quad \mathbb E[H]=\frac{n}{2\beta}.$$

Positive definiteness and $\beta>0$ are essential for this normalized full-space Gaussian. The unrestricted identity $\mathbb E[x\,H'(x)]=\beta^{-1}$ is false without a boundary hypothesis: on $[-L,L]$ with $L>0$ and $H\equiv0$, the normalized expectation on the left is $0$.
items.strategy:
1.1 We construct $R$ with $K=R^{\mathsf T}R$ by induction on $n$. For $n=1$, take $R=\sqrt{K_{11}}>0$. For $n>1$, write $K=\begin{pmatrix}a&b^{\mathsf T}\\b&C\end{pmatrix}$; positive definiteness gives $a>0$ and $S:=C-bb^{\mathsf T}/a$ positive definite, since $y^{\mathsf T}Sy=(-b^{\mathsf T}y/a,y)^{\mathsf T}K(-b^{\mathsf T}y/a,y)>0$ for $y\ne0$. By induction $S=R_1^{\mathsf T}R_1$; then $R=\begin{pmatrix}\sqrt a&b^{\mathsf T}/\sqrt a\\0&R_1\end{pmatrix}$ satisfies $R^{\mathsf T}R=K$. Its diagonal entries are positive, so $\det R>0$; taking determinants gives $\det K=(\det R)^2$ and therefore $\det R=\sqrt{\det K}$. [given, construct, algebra]

2.1 Put $T(x)=Rx$. This is a $C^1$ diffeomorphism of $\mathbb R^n$ with $|\det DT|=\det R$. Since $H(x)=|Rx|^2/2$, [F2] gives $$Z=(\det R)^{-1}\int_{\mathbb R^n}e^{-\beta|y|^2/2}\,d\lambda_n(y).$$ By [F3], $\lambda_n$ is the finite product of $n$ sigma-finite one-dimensional Lebesgue measures; Tonelli and the factorization $e^{-\beta|y|^2/2}=\prod_i e^{-\beta y_i^2/2}$ give the integral as $I_0(\beta/2)^n$. By [F1] and [F4], $I_0(\beta/2)=\sqrt{2\pi/\beta}$. Hence $$Z=(2\pi/\beta)^{n/2}(\det K)^{-1/2},$$ which is finite and positive. [given, F1, F2, F3, F4, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 Let $Y$ have the normalized density proportional to $e^{-\beta|y|^2/2}$ with respect to $\lambda_n$. For each $i$, [F3] and Tonelli factor the nonnegative second-moment integral into $I_1(\beta/2)I_0(\beta/2)^{n-1}$, while the normalizer is $I_0(\beta/2)^n$; [F1] gives $\mathbb E[Y_i^2]=I_1(\beta/2)/I_0(\beta/2)=1/\beta$. Also $\int |y_i|e^{-\beta|y|^2/2}d\lambda_n<\infty$, since $|y_i|\le1+y_i^2$ and the same Tonelli factorization makes both integrals finite. For $i\ne j$, $|y_iy_j|\le(y_i^2+y_j^2)/2$, so the cross moments are absolutely integrable. Fubini [F3] factors these signed moments; the one-dimensional first and odd moments vanish by [F1]. Thus $\mathbb E[Y]=0$ and $\mathbb E[YY^{\mathsf T}]=\beta^{-1}I$. [F1, F3, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 By [F2], the normalized law of $X$ is the pullback of the law of $Y$ under $x=R^{-1}y$. The absolute integrability established in step 3.1 permits the same change of variables for signed first and second moments by applying [F2] to their positive and negative parts. Hence $\mathbb E[X]=0$ and $$\mathbb E[XX^{\mathsf T}]=R^{-1}(\beta^{-1}I)R^{-\mathsf T}=\beta^{-1}(R^{\mathsf T}R)^{-1}=\beta^{-1}K^{-1}.$$ Since $H(X)=|Y|^2/2$, summing the diagonal second moments gives $\mathbb E[H]=n/(2\beta)$. [F2, step 1.1, step 3.1, algebra]

5.1 For the stated boundary counterexample, the density on $[-L,L]$ is the constant $(2L)^{-1}$ because $H=0$ and the normalizing integral is $2L$ by [F3]. Since $H'(x)=0$ everywhere, $\mathbb E[xH'(x)]=0\ne\beta^{-1}$ for $\beta>0$. [given, F3, algebra] ∎

references.title: Michael E. Taylor, Introduction to Analysis in Several Variables (Advanced Calculus), §3.1
David Tong, Statistical Physics, §2.2.1, equipartition of quadratic degrees of freedom

items.title: Exact spherical-shell coordinate marginal and fixed-block Gaussian limit
items.design_state: Initial authoring complete; current prerequisite availability and readiness disposition are recorded in batch evidence.
items.statement:
Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ as defined in [[def-countable-choice]]. Let $D\ge2$, $1\le k<D$, and $R>0$. Let $Z_1,\ldots,Z_D$ be independent real random variables with common Lebesgue probability density $\phi(x):=(2\pi)^{-1/2}e^{-x^2/2}$; its integral is one by the Gaussian integral in [[lem-csm-examples-gamma-gaussian-tools]], and this is the standard-normal coordinate law. Set $Z=(Z_1,\ldots,Z_D)$ and define $P:=RZ/|Z|$ when $Z\ne0$, and $P:=0$ when $Z=0$. The joint density of $Z$ makes $\mathbb P(Z=0)=0$. The distribution of $P$ is rotationally invariant, meaning that for every orthogonal map $Q\in O(D)$ and Borel set $A\subseteq\mathbb R^D$, $\mathbb P(QP\in A)=\mathbb P(P\in A)$. It is concentrated on the sphere in the precise sense that $\mathbb P(|P|=R)=1$. Its first $k$ coordinates have Lebesgue density

$$f_{D,k}(y)=\frac{\Gamma(D/2)}{\Gamma((D-k)/2)(\pi R^2)^{k/2}}\left(1-\frac{|y|^2}{R^2}\right)^{(D-k-2)/2}\quad (|y|<R),$$

and zero for $|y|\ge R$. This density is integrable even when it diverges at the boundary. Also $\mathbb E[P_i]=0$, $\mathbb E[P_iP_j]=0$ for $i\ne j$, and $\mathbb E[P_i^2]=R^2/D$.

For fixed $k$ and $\sigma>0$, set $R_D=\sqrt D\,\sigma$ and let $D\to\infty$ through integers $D>k$. If $g:\mathbb R^k\to\mathbb R$ is bounded and Lipschitz in the Euclidean norm, meaning that finite constants $B_g,L_g$ satisfy $|g(x)|\le B_g$ and $|g(x)-g(y)|\le L_g|x-y|$ for all $x,y\in\mathbb R^k$, then

$$\mathbb E\,g\bigl((P_1,\ldots,P_k)\bigr)\longrightarrow\mathbb E\,g\bigl(\sigma(Z_1,\ldots,Z_k)\bigr).$$

This is a fixed-block bounded-Lipschitz test limit; it makes no claim uniform in $k$ or for unbounded test functions. If $k=D$, the projection is singular on the sphere and the displayed Lebesgue density is not asserted.
items.strategy:
1.1 The joint density of $Z$ is $(2\pi)^{-D/2}e^{-|z|^2/2}$. For every orthogonal $Q$, the substitution $z\mapsto Qz$ has absolute determinant $1$ and preserves $|z|$, so $QZ$ has the same law as $Z$. Therefore $P=RZ/|Z|$ is rotationally invariant and satisfies $|P|=R$ almost surely. [given, F1, F2, algebra]



1.2 Write $Z=(A,B)$ with $A\in\mathbb R^k$ and $B\in\mathbb R^{D-k}$. The vectors are independent. By the one-coordinate substitution $w=Z_j^2/2$, each $w$ has gamma density $w^{-1/2}e^{-w}/\Gamma(1/2)$; repeated application of [F1] shows $T:=|B|^2$ has density $t^{b-1}e^{-t/2}/(2^b\Gamma(b))$ for $t>0$, where $b=(D-k)/2$, independently of $A$. [F1, algebra]



1.3 For fixed $t>0$, the first $k$ coordinates $y=RA/\sqrt{|A|^2+t}$ range over $|y|<R$. The inverse is $A=\sqrt t\,y/\sqrt{R^2-|y|^2}$. Its derivative has radial eigenvalue $\sqrt t\,R^2/(R^2-|y|^2)^{3/2}$ and $k-1$ tangential eigenvalues $\sqrt t/(R^2-|y|^2)^{1/2}$, hence Jacobian $t^{k/2}R^2/(R^2-|y|^2)^{k/2+1}$. [given, construct, algebra]



2.1 The map $(y,t)\mapsto(A(y,t),t)$ is a $C^1$ diffeomorphism from $\{|y|<R,t>0\}$ to $\mathbb R^k\times(0,\infty)$. Apply [F2] first on compact subsets away from $t=0$ and $|y|=R$ and then take increasing nonnegative limits. Substituting the Gaussian density of $A$, the gamma density of $T$, and the Jacobian from step 1.3 gives $f_{D,k}(y)=\frac{R^2}{(2\pi)^{k/2}2^b\Gamma(b)(R^2-|y|^2)^{k/2+1}}\int_0^\infty t^{D/2-1}\exp\!\left(-\frac{tR^2}{2(R^2-|y|^2)}\right)dt$. The substitution $u=tR^2/[2(R^2-|y|^2)]$ evaluates the integral as $\Gamma(D/2)[2(R^2-|y|^2)/R^2]^{D/2}$. Since $D/2=k/2+b$, simplification gives the displayed density. The boundary singularity, when present, has exponent $b-1>-1$ in the radial variable and is integrable; the pushforward construction and $\mathbb P(Z=0)=0$ show the density has total mass one and no boundary atom. [F1, F2, step 1.2, step 1.3, algebra]



2.2 Sign changes of one Gaussian coordinate show $\mathbb E[P_i]=0$ and $\mathbb E[P_iP_j]=0$ for $i\ne j$. Permutation invariance makes all $\mathbb E[P_i^2]$ equal, while $\sum_{i=1}^D P_i^2=R^2$ almost surely; summing expectations gives $\mathbb E[P_i^2]=R^2/D$. [step 1.1, given, algebra]



3.1 For each finite $D$, take the product Gaussian vector $Z=(Z_1,\ldots,Z_D)$ in that dimension and set $S_D:=D^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^D Z_i^2$. By [F1] and independence, $\mathbb E S_D=1$, $\mathbb E[(S_D-1)^2]=2/D$, and $\mathbb E|Z_{1:k}|^2=k$. Fix $0<\delta<1/2$ and $M>0$. On $E_D=\{|Z_{1:k}|\le M,\ |S_D-1|\le\delta\}$, the derivative of $u^{-1/2}$ is bounded by $\sqrt2$ on $[1/2,3/2]$, so $|\sigma Z_{1:k}/\sqrt{S_D}-\sigma Z_{1:k}|\le\sqrt2\sigma M\delta$. If $g$ is bounded Lipschitz with bound $B_g$ and Lipschitz constant $L_g$, then $M^2\mathbf 1_{\{|Z_{1:k}|>M\}}\le |Z_{1:k}|^2$ and $\delta^2\mathbf 1_{\{|S_D-1|>\delta\}}\le(S_D-1)^2$ imply $\mathbb P(E_D^c)\le k/M^2+2/(D\delta^2)$. Therefore $|\mathbb E g(P_{1:k})-\mathbb E g(\sigma Z_{1:k})|\le L_g\sqrt2\sigma M\delta+2B_g\left(\frac{k}{M^2}+\frac{2}{D\delta^2}\right)$. Choose $M$ large, then $\delta$ small, then $D$ large. The right side becomes arbitrarily small, proving the stated test convergence without assuming independence between $Z_{1:k}$ and $S_D$. [F1, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

references.title: Michael E. Taylor, Introduction to Analysis in Several Variables (Advanced Calculus), §3.1
NIST Digital Library of Mathematical Functions, §5.2(i), Euler's integral
Mehran Kardar, MIT OpenCourseWare 8.333, Statistical Mechanics I, Lecture 13 (Fall 2013), IV.D

items.title: Declared example preparations and thermodynamic interpretation
items.design_state: Initial authoring complete; current prerequisite availability and readiness disposition are recorded in batch evidence.
items.statement:
Here $\log$ denotes the natural logarithm defined in [[def-natural-logarithm]].

For each named finite classical model in this page, adopt the preparation explicitly stated in its theorem. In a canonical branch, take a measurable phase space with a specified reference measure $\nu$, a measurable Hamiltonian $H$, an inverse energy parameter $\beta>0$, and a finite positive partition function $Z=\int e^{-\beta H}\,d\nu$; the adopted probability measure is $dP=Z^{-1}e^{-\beta H}\,d\nu$. In a grand-canonical branch, take disjoint particle-number sectors with sector partition functions $Z_N$ and a dimensionless activity $z>0$ for which $\Xi=\sum_{N\ge0}z^N Z_N$ is finite; sector $N$ has probability weight $z^N Z_N/\Xi$. The spherical-shell and product preparations are separate explicitly specified probability laws in their consuming theorem statements. These are alternative model assumptions, not consequences of a Hamiltonian flow and not assertions that a laboratory system realizes them.

For a canonical model whose reference measure and Hamiltonian are fixed, adopt the statistical thermodynamic definitions $U=\mathbb E_P[H]$, $F=-\beta^{-1}\log Z$, and $S=k_B(\log Z+\beta U)$ when the displayed integrals are finite. For a volume-dependent model, define the model pressure as $-\partial_V F$ only along the declared fixed-shape volume family. Here $k_B>0$ has SI units J K$^{-1}$, temperature $T>0$ has units K, and $\beta=(k_BT)^{-1}$ has units J$^{-1}$. The fixed reference measure is part of the preparation; changing it changes the numerical partition function and entropy convention.

For the continuous particle examples, adopt the operational species and
counting convention of [[post-csm-counting-and-physical-observables]]. Use
one fixed primitive action reference $a_0>0$ in J s, and write $h_0:=a_0$
where the consuming model uses the notation $h_0$. In a Cartesian physical
phase chart $dq\,dp$ has action dimension $(\mathrm{J\,s})^{dN}$, so the
reference $dq\,dp/(\prod_sN_s!\,a_0^{dN})$ is dimensionless. Each model
retains its declared operational labels: an omitted factorial for resolved
harmonic coordinates is not replaced by a particle-exchange quotient. The
finite spin examples use their stated discrete counting measure, without a
continuous phase-cell factor. Choosing a numerical reference action, or
identifying it with Planck's constant, is an additional convention; no such
value or identification is imposed here. The Gaussian and gamma identities
in [[lem-csm-examples-gamma-gaussian-tools]] establish the mathematical
normalizations, not the physical preparation or empirical equilibration.

references.title: David Tong, Statistical Physics, §§1.2–1.5 and §2.2
Mehran Kardar, MIT OpenCourseWare 8.333, Statistical Mechanics I, Lecture 14, §§IV.G and IV.I (Fall 2013)

items.physical_scope: Separate finite classical canonical, grand-canonical, spherical-shell and product preparations in the named model examples; no claim of equilibration, empirical truth, or statistical inference from observations.

items.title: Confined coupled quadratic canonical systems
items.design_state: Initial authoring complete; current prerequisite availability and readiness disposition are recorded in batch evidence.
items.statement:
Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ as defined in [[def-countable-choice]] for the Euclidean Lebesgue product measure used below. Let $n\ge1$, let $M=\operatorname{diag}(m_1,\ldots,m_n)$ with $m_i>0$ in kg, and let $K$ be a real symmetric positive-definite stiffness matrix with entries in J m$^{-2}$. For displacement $q\in\mathbb R^n$ in metres and momentum $p\in\mathbb R^n$ in kg m s$^{-1}$, define
$$H(q,p)=\tfrac12p^{\mathsf T}M^{-1}p+\tfrac12q^{\mathsf T}Kq.$$
Adopt the canonical probability density proportional to $e^{-\beta H}$ relative to $dq\,dp/h_0^n$, where $\beta>0$ has units J$^{-1}$ and the fixed action reference $h_0>0$ has units J s. Under the preparation of [[post-csm-examples-ensemble-preparations]], the dimensionless partition function and moments are
$$Z=\left(\frac{2\pi}{\beta h_0}\right)^n\sqrt{\frac{\det M}{\det K}},\quad \mathbb E[q]=\mathbb E[p]=0,\quad \mathbb E[qq^{\mathsf T}]=\beta^{-1}K^{-1},\quad \mathbb E[pp^{\mathsf T}]=\beta^{-1}M,\quad \mathbb E[qp^{\mathsf T}]=0.$$
The model mean energy is $U=\mathbb E[H]=n/\beta$. With $k_B>0$ in J K$^{-1}$ and $T>0$ in K from [[post-csm-examples-ensemble-preparations]], so that $\beta=(k_BT)^{-1}$, define the fixed-parameter heat-capacity response by
$$C_{\mathrm{harm}}:=\left(\frac{\partial U}{\partial T}\right)_{M,K,h_0}=nk_B.$$
It has units J K$^{-1}$. This model has no volume variable, so $C_{\mathrm{harm}}$ is not a fixed-volume derivative.
items.strategy:
1.1 By [F1], the phase-space weight factors as $e^{-\beta p^{\mathsf T}M^{-1}p/2}e^{-\beta q^{\mathsf T}Kq/2}$. The product-measure identity and Tonelli [F3] justify multiplying the two nonnegative Lebesgue integrals. Applying [F2] to the $q$ factor gives normalization $(2\pi/\beta)^{n/2}(\det K)^{-1/2}$ and covariance $\beta^{-1}K^{-1}$. [given, F1, F2, F3, algebra]



1.2 The momentum quadratic form has symmetric positive-definite matrix $M^{-1}$. Applying [F2] with $K=M^{-1}$ gives its integral $(2\pi/\beta)^{n/2}\sqrt{\det M}$ and covariance of $p$ equal to $\beta^{-1}(M^{-1})^{-1}=\beta^{-1}M$. [given, F2, algebra]



2.1 Multiplying the two integrals from steps 1.1–1.2 and dividing by the reference factor $h_0^n$ gives $Z=(2\pi/(\beta h_0))^n\sqrt{\det M/\det K}$. The phase-space Lebesgue measure is the product of its $q$ and $p$ factors by [F3]; the normalized canonical density therefore factors into independent $q$ and $p$ laws. Each factor is even, so its mean is zero, and its covariance is the one computed in steps 1.1–1.2. [A1, F3, step 1.1, step 1.2, algebra]



3.1 By [F1], taking the expectation of $H$ and summing the diagonal traces of the two covariance identities gives $$U=\tfrac12\mathbb E[p^{\mathsf T}M^{-1}p]+\tfrac12\mathbb E[q^{\mathsf T}Kq]=\frac{n}{2\beta}+\frac{n}{2\beta}=\frac{n}{\beta}.$$ The adopted relation $\beta^{-1}=k_BT$ makes $U=nk_BT$. Holding the model parameters $M,K,h_0$ fixed therefore gives $C_{\mathrm{harm}}=(\partial U/\partial T)_{M,K,h_0}=nk_B$, with units J K$^{-1}$. [A1, F1, step 1.1, step 1.2, algebra] ∎
