items.physical_scope: Finite classical continuous canonical model with positive diagonal mass matrix, strictly positive stiffness matrix, fixed positive action reference and beta>0; the Lebesgue product calculations assume ACω; no unpinned zero mode or empirical equilibration claim.

items.title: Exact canonical and grand ideal-gas preparations
items.design_state: Initial authoring complete; current prerequisite availability and readiness disposition are recorded in batch evidence.
items.statement:
Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ as defined in [[def-countable-choice]], for the Euclidean Lebesgue product and polar-coordinate suppliers used below. Let $\exp(x):=\sum_{n=0}^\infty x^n/n!$ be the real exponential of [[def-real-exponential-function-and-e]], and let $\log$ be the natural logarithm of [[def-natural-logarithm]], with $\log'(x)=1/x$ for $x>0$ by [[thm-logarithm-derivative-and-integral]]. Let $d,N\ge1$ and let $B=\prod_{j=1}^d[0,L_j]\subset\mathbb R^d$, where each side length $L_j>0$ is in metres and $V:=\prod_jL_j$ is in $\mathrm m^d$. Let $m>0$ be the common particle mass in kg, $\beta>0$ in J$^{-1}$, and let $h_0:=a_0>0$ be the fixed action reference in J s from [[post-csm-examples-ensemble-preparations]]. Take one species of $N$ operationally indistinguishable particles as in [[post-csm-counting-and-physical-observables]]. On its auxiliary labelled cover, positions $q_i\in B$ are in metres and momenta $p_i\in\mathbb R^d$ are in kg m s$^{-1}$; the Hamiltonian is permutation invariant and the reference measure is
$$d\nu_N=\frac{dq\,dp}{N!h_0^{dN}}.$$
The symmetric labelled law represents the quotient preparation; a one-particle marginal below means the law of a uniformly selected particle. For $N\ge1$, define
$$H_N(q,p)=\sum_{i=1}^N\frac{|p_i|^2}{2m}$$
and use the canonical preparation of [[post-csm-examples-ensemble-preparations]]. For the vacuum sector $N=0$, define $B^0\times\mathbb R^{d\cdot0}$ to be a singleton with reference measure $\nu_0=1$, set $H_0=0$, and use empty-product conventions $V^0=0!=h_0^0=1$; thus $Z_0=1$. The mass parameter $m$ applies when particles are present; the vacuum sector has no mass coordinate. For all $N\ge0$, set $\lambda:=h_0\sqrt{\beta/(2\pi m)}$ (metres) and
$$Z_N=\int e^{-\beta H_N}\,d\nu_N=\frac{V^N}{N!\lambda^{dN}}.$$
For $N\ge1$, the labelled-cover position coordinates are independent uniform points of $B$ and are independent of the momenta; all momentum components are independent centered Gaussians of variance $m/\beta$. The joint law is permutation invariant. The energy satisfies $U=\mathbb E H_N=dN/(2\beta)$ and $\operatorname{Var}(H_N)=dN/(2\beta^2)$, with variance in J$^2$. With the adopted Boltzmann constant $k_B>0$ in J K$^{-1}$ and temperature $T:=(k_B\beta)^{-1}>0$ in K from [[post-csm-examples-ensemble-preparations]], define $F=-\beta^{-1}\log Z_N$ and scale all box side lengths uniformly when varying $V$, holding the shape, $N,T,d,m,h_0$ fixed. The model pressure $\mathcal P:=-\left(\partial F/\partial V\right)_{N,T,d,m,h_0,\,\mathrm{shape}}$ has units J m$^{-d}$ (equivalently N m$^{1-d}$; Pa when $d=3$) and obeys $\mathcal PV=N/\beta=Nk_BT$. The fixed-reference entropy is $S=k_B(\log Z_N+\beta U)$ and retains the chosen $N!$ and $h_0$ convention.

For $d=3$, the speed $v=|p|/m$ of a uniformly selected particle, in m s$^{-1}$, has density
$$f(v)=4\pi\left(\frac{m\beta}{2\pi}\right)^{3/2}v^2e^{-\beta mv^2/2},\qquad v\ge0.$$
Its squared-speed expectation, modal speed, and mean speed are $\mathbb E[v^2]=3/(m\beta)$ in m$^2$ s$^{-2}$, $\sqrt{2/(m\beta)}$ in m s$^{-1}$, and $\mathbb E[v]=\sqrt{8/(\pi m\beta)}$ in m s$^{-1}$, respectively.

For the separate grand-canonical preparation of [[post-csm-examples-ensemble-preparations]] on disjoint number sectors $N\in\{0,1,\ldots\}$, whose sector weights are proportional to $z^NZ_N$, let $\mu_{\rm chem}$ be a chemical potential in joules and $z=\exp(\beta\mu_{\rm chem})>0$ the dimensionless activity. Then
$$\Xi=\sum_{N=0}^\infty z^NZ_N=\exp(zV/\lambda^d),\qquad \mathbb P(N=j)=\exp(-\nu)\frac{\nu^j}{j!},\quad \nu:=zV/\lambda^d,$$
so $\mathbb E N=\operatorname{Var}(N)=\nu$ and the conditional law given $N$ is the canonical law above.

A distinct three-dimensional classical ultra-relativistic model adopts $H_{\rm ur}(p)=c|p|$ for every $p\in\mathbb R^3$, with $c>0$ in m s$^{-1}$ and $p$ in kg m s$^{-1}$, in the same box volume $V$ in m$^3$. This extends the nonzero massless momentum formula continuously to $p=0$ only to define a density on all of $\mathbb R^3$; the point has Lebesgue measure zero and no physical zero-momentum massless state is asserted. Its separate canonical partition function is
$$Z_{N,{\rm ur}}=\frac{V^N}{N!h_0^{3N}}\left(\frac{8\pi}{(\beta c)^3}\right)^N,$$
with $U_{\rm ur}=3N/\beta$ J and $\operatorname{Var}(H_{\rm ur})=3N/\beta^2$ J$^2$. Define its fixed-volume heat capacity by $C_{V,\rm ur}:=(\partial U_{\rm ur}/\partial T)_{V,N,c,h_0}=3Nk_B$; it has units J K$^{-1}$. Its three-dimensional pressure obeys $\mathcal PV=N/\beta$ and has units Pa. This branch is not obtained by setting $m=0$ in the Gaussian model and makes no photon-number or quantum-statistics claim.
items.strategy:
**Given:** $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, $d,N\ge1$, the rectangular box $B$ with side lengths in metres and volume $V$ in $\mathrm m^d$, one operationally indistinguishable species, $m>0$ kg, $h_0=a_0>0$ J s, $\beta>0$ J$^{-1}$, and the Hamiltonian and symmetric reference measure in the Statement.

1.1 By [F3], Euclidean Lebesgue measure in the position and momentum coordinates is their product measure; [F5] then factors the nonnegative normalization integral. The box-volume formula [F4] gives $\lambda_{dN}(B^N)=V^N$. Each of the $dN$ scalar momentum factors contributes $\int_{\mathbb R}e^{-\beta p^2/(2m)}dp=\sqrt{2\pi m/\beta}$ by [F2] and [F7]. Including the stipulated factor $1/(N!h_0^{dN})$ from [F12] yields $Z_N=V^N(N!h_0^{dN})^{-1}(2\pi m/\beta)^{dN/2}=V^N/(N!\lambda^{dN})$. [given, F1, F2, F3, F4, F5, F7, F12, algebra]

1.2 For the separate massless branch, let $N_{\rm time}$ denote the background's smooth future-timelike field $N$ from [F10] and normalize it at the event by $n=N_{\rm time}/\sqrt{-g(N_{\rm time},N_{\rm time})}$. [F8] makes $P$ future null, so $g(P,n)<0$. By [F11], $|q_n(P)|^2=g(q_n(P),q_n(P))=g(P,n)^2$, hence $E_n(P)=-cg(P,n)=c|q_n(P)|$. Identifying $q_n$ with its components in an orthonormal basis of the positive rest space gives the adopted $H_{\rm ur}(p)=c|p|$ with the stated units. [given, A2, F8, F9, F10, F11, algebra]

2.1 After normalization, the canonical density is the product of the uniform position density on $B^N$ and the $dN$ scalar Gaussian momentum densities. For measurable coordinate rectangles, [F3] and [F5] show their probabilities factor; hence the positions and all momentum components are independent, each position is uniform on $B$, and each momentum component is centered with variance $m/\beta$ by [F2]. [given, F2, F3, F5, step 1.1]

2.2 In the grand preparation of [F1], use the vacuum convention $Z_0=1$ and substitute $Z_N=V^N/(N!\lambda^{dN})$ for all $N\ge0$ into the sector sum. With $\nu=zV/\lambda^d$, [F13] gives $\Xi=\sum_{N\ge0}\nu^N/N!=\exp(\nu)$, and [F14] gives the normalized sector weight $\nu^N/(N!\exp(\nu))=\exp(-\nu)\nu^N/N!$. [A1, F1, F13, F14, step 1.1, algebra]

2.3 By [F6], the momentum integral for one ultra-relativistic particle is $$\int_{\mathbb R^3}e^{-\beta c|p|}\,d\lambda_3(p)=4\pi\int_0^\infty r^2e^{-\beta cr}dr=4\pi\frac{\Gamma(3)}{(\beta c)^3}=\frac{8\pi}{(\beta c)^3},$$ using [F2]. The point $p=0$ is Lebesgue null by [F18], so the continuous extension adds no massless zero-momentum state. Product measure and Tonelli [F3, F5] give the $N$-particle product, and the stated positional/counting reference then gives $Z_{N,\rm ur}$. [A1, A2, F1, F2, F3, F5, F6, F18, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 Each scalar momentum coordinate has second moment $m/\beta$ and fourth moment $3m^2/\beta^2$ from [F2]. Thus each term $p_{i\alpha}^2/(2m)$ has mean $1/(2\beta)$ and variance $1/(2\beta^2)$; independence from step 2.1 makes means and variances add, giving the stated $U$ and $\operatorname{Var}(H_N)$. [given, F2, step 2.1, algebra]

3.2 For $d=3$, write $a=\beta/(2m)$. The one-particle momentum density is $(a/\pi)^{3/2}e^{-a|p|^2}$. By [F6], for every Borel $A\subseteq[0,\infty)$ the probability that $v=|p|/m$ lies in $A$ is $$4\pi(a/\pi)^{3/2}\int_{mA}r^2e^{-ar^2}\,dr.$$ The substitution $r=mv$ therefore gives the speed density $4\pi(m\beta/(2\pi))^{3/2}v^2e^{-\beta mv^2/2}$ on $v\ge0$. [given, F2, F6, step 2.1, algebra]

3.3 Shifting the index in the absolutely convergent series [F13] gives $\sum_{j\ge0}j\nu^j/j!=\nu\exp(\nu)$ and $\sum_{j\ge0}j(j-1)\nu^j/j!=\nu^2\exp(\nu)$. After normalization by [F14], $\mathbb E N=\nu$ and $\mathbb E[N(N-1)]=\nu^2$, hence $\operatorname{Var}(N)=\mathbb E[N(N-1)]+\mathbb EN-(\mathbb EN)^2=\nu$. Conditioning on sector $N$ recovers the canonical density because its factor $z^N$ is constant within that sector. [F13, F14, step 2.2, algebra]

4.1 By [F17] and [A1], $F=-\beta^{-1}[N\log(V/\lambda^d)-\log N!]$ for fixed $T,N$ and fixed box shape. The log derivative [F16] gives $-\partial_VF=N/(\beta V)$, with $\mathcal P$ in J m$^{-d}$, and therefore $\mathcal PV=N/\beta$. The entropy definition in [F1] gives $S=k_B(\log Z_N+\beta U)$ with the same fixed $h_0$ and factorial convention. [A1, F1, F15, F16, F17, step 1.1, step 3.1, algebra]

4.2 The speed density is proportional to $v^2e^{-av^2}$ with $a=\beta m/2$. Its derivative has the sign of $2v(1-av^2)$ for $v>0$, so its unique positive maximum occurs at $v_{\rm mode}=a^{-1/2}$. The second moment is $3/(2a)=3/(m\beta)$ by the gamma recurrence in [F2]. The mean is $$\mathbb E v=\frac{4a^{3/2}}{\sqrt\pi}\int_0^\infty v^3e^{-av^2}dv=\frac{4a^{3/2}}{\sqrt\pi}\frac{\Gamma(2)}{2a^2}=\frac{2}{\sqrt{\pi a}}=\sqrt{\frac{8}{\pi\beta m}}.$$ These are model-distribution moments, not values for an individual measured particle. [F2, step 3.2, algebra]

5.1 Under the normalized radial density proportional to $r^2e^{-\beta cr}$, gamma moments give mean energy $3/\beta$ and variance $3/\beta^2$ per particle. Independence from the product preparation adds these to $U_{\rm ur}=3N/\beta$ and $\operatorname{Var}(H_{\rm ur})=3N/\beta^2$; differentiating at fixed $V,N,c,h_0$ with $\beta^{-1}=k_BT$ gives $C_{V,\rm ur}=3Nk_B$ J K$^{-1}$. Since $Z_{N,\rm ur}$ is proportional to $V^N$, [F16] gives $-\partial_VF=N/(\beta V)$ and $\mathcal PV=N/\beta$, with $\mathcal P$ in Pa for this three-dimensional branch. [A1, F1, F2, F5, F16, step 2.3, algebra] ∎

items.title: Finite periodic Ising-ring correlations and exact decay
items.design_state: Initial authoring complete; current prerequisite availability and readiness disposition are recorded in batch evidence.
items.statement:
Use the real exponential $\exp(x)=\sum_{n\ge0}x^n/n!$ of [[def-real-exponential-function-and-e]] and the hyperbolic functions $\cosh x=(\exp x+\exp(-x))/2$, $\sinh x=(\exp x-\exp(-x))/2$. Define $\tanh x:=\sinh x/\cosh x$; the denominator is positive for every real $x$. Let $N\ge2$, let $\Omega_N=\{-1,1\}^N$ with cyclic indexing $s_{N+1}=s_1$, and count exactly the $N$ indexed periodic bonds (so $N=2$ has two bonds). For coupling $J\ge0$ in joules, zero field, and $\beta>0$ in J$^{-1}$, adopt the finite canonical law
$$\mathbb P_N(s)=Z_N^{-1}\exp\!\left(\beta J\sum_{i=1}^Ns_is_{i+1}\right).$$
Set $t=\tanh(\beta J)\in[0,1)$. For $1\le r\le N-1$,
$$\mathbb E_N[s_i]=0,\qquad \mathbb E_N[s_i s_{i+r}]=\frac{t^r+t^{N-r}}{1+t^N}.$$
For each fixed positive integer separation $r$ and $N\to\infty$, the correlation tends to $t^r$, with absolute error at most $t^{N-r}+t^{N+r}$. When $J>0$, define the limiting correlation length $\xi>0$ in lattice spacings as the unique number satisfying $t^r=e^{-r/\xi}$ for every positive integer separation $r$; equivalently, $\xi=-1/\log t$. The zero-field susceptibility per spin, defined by $\chi_N:=N^{-1}\partial_h\mathbb E_{N,h}[\sum_i s_i]|_{h=0}$ for the field-coupled law with energy $-\!J\sum_i s_is_{i+1}-h\sum_i s_i$, where the field parameter $h\in\mathbb R$ is in joules, has limit
$$\chi_\infty=\beta\frac{1+t}{1-t}.$$
Both $\chi_N$ and $\chi_\infty$ have units J$^{-1}$ per spin (the spin variables are dimensionless).
Define the finite-ring model free energy by $F_N:=-\beta^{-1}\log Z_N$ and its limiting free energy per spin, when the limit exists, by $f_\infty:=\lim_{N\to\infty}F_N/N$. Then $f_\infty=-\beta^{-1}\log(2\cosh(\beta J))$, analytic at every finite positive temperature. No statement is made for arbitrary one-dimensional interactions.
items.strategy:
1.1 In the zero-field case the transfer matrix in [F2] is $T_{s,t}=e^{Kst}$ with $K=\beta J$, so $T=\begin{pmatrix}e^K&e^{-K}\\e^{-K}&e^K\end{pmatrix}$. Direct multiplication gives orthonormal eigenvectors $u_+=(1,1)/\sqrt2$, $u_-=(1,-1)/\sqrt2$ with eigenvalues $\lambda_+=2\cosh K$ and $\lambda_-=2\sinh K$. Hence $Z_N=\operatorname{tr}(T^N)=\lambda_+^N+\lambda_-^N=\lambda_+^N(1+t^N)$, where $t=\lambda_-/\lambda_+=\tanh K$. [given, F2, algebra]



2.1 By the finite preparation [F1], the partition sum is the normalization for the adopted law. Put $D_0=\operatorname{diag}(1,-1)$; then $D_0u_+=u_-$ and $D_0u_-=u_+$. Expanding the finite canonical sum over the $N$ cyclic indices with $s_i s_{i+r}$ inserted gives numerator $\operatorname{tr}(D_0T^rD_0T^{N-r})$. Evaluating this trace in the eigenbasis yields $\lambda_-^r\lambda_+^{N-r}+\lambda_+^r\lambda_-^{N-r}$. Dividing by $Z_N$ from step 1.1 gives the stated correlation formula. [A1, F1, F2, step 1.1, algebra]



3.1 The map $s\mapsto-s$ preserves every bond product and reverses $\sum_i s_i$, so at zero field $\mathbb E_N[s_i]=0$. For fixed $r$, subtracting $t^r$ from the formula of step 2.1 gives $(t^{N-r}-t^{N+r})/(1+t^N)$; its absolute value is at most $t^{N-r}+t^{N+r}$ because $0\le t<1$. Thus the fixed-distance limit is $t^r$. When $0<t<1$, writing $t^r=e^{-r/\xi}$ gives $\xi=-1/\log t$; for $J=0$, $t=0$ and all nonzero-separation correlations vanish. [step 2.1, algebra]



3.2 For the field-coupled finite law [A1], differentiating its finite numerator and denominator sums gives $\partial_h\mathbb E_{N,h}[M]=\beta(\mathbb E_{N,h}[M^2]-\mathbb E_{N,h}[M]^2)$, where $M=\sum_i s_i$. At $h=0$, spin-flip symmetry gives $\mathbb E M=0$ and translation invariance gives $$\frac1N\mathbb E[M^2]=1+\sum_{r=1}^{N-1}\mathbb E[s_1s_{1+r}]=1+\frac{2\sum_{r=1}^{N-1}t^r}{1+t^N}.$$ The finite geometric sum tends to $2t/(1-t)$ as $N\to\infty$, so $\chi_N\to\beta(1+t)/(1-t)$. This also gives $\chi_N=\beta$ when $J=0$. [A1, step 2.1, algebra]



4.1 From step 1.1, $N^{-1}\log Z_N=\log(2\cosh(\beta J))+N^{-1}\log(1+t^N)$. Since $1\le1+t^N\le2$, the second term tends to zero; the limit is analytic for every finite $\beta>0$ because $\cosh(\beta J)>0$. The correlation length diverges only in the excluded zero-temperature limit $\beta J\to\infty$. [step 1.1, step 3.1, algebra] ∎

items.title: Exact Tonks hard-rod pressure and convergent virial series
items.design_state: Initial authoring complete; current prerequisite availability and readiness disposition are recorded in batch evidence.
items.statement:
Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ as defined in [[def-countable-choice]] for the Euclidean Lebesgue product and Jordan-volume identifications below. Use the natural logarithm $\log$ of [[def-natural-logarithm]]. Let $N\ge1$, let $a\ge0$ be a hard-rod length in metres, and let $L>Na$ be the one-dimensional box length in metres. Rod centers are $x_i\in[a/2,L-a/2]$ with $|x_i-x_j|\ge a$ for $i\ne j$. Let each rod have mass $m>0$ kg, momentum $p_i\in\mathbb R$ in kg m s$^{-1}$, and Hamiltonian $H=\sum_{i=1}^Np_i^2/(2m)$ on the allowed configuration set, with infinite energy outside it. Adopt the reference $dx\,dp/(N!h_0^N)$, where $h_0>0$ is a fixed action in J s, and canonical inverse temperature $\beta>0$ in J$^{-1}$. Put $\lambda=h_0\sqrt{\beta/(2\pi m)}$. Then
$$Z_N=\frac{(L-Na)^N}{N!\lambda^N},\quad U=\mathbb E H=\frac{N}{2\beta},\quad p_{1D}:=-\left(\frac{\partial F}{\partial L}\right)_{N,a,m,\beta,h_0}=\frac{N}{\beta(L-Na)},\quad F=-\beta^{-1}\log Z_N.$$
Here $p_{1D}$ is the one-dimensional force conjugate to length and has units N; it is not a three-dimensional pressure. With number density $\rho=N/L$, the exact equation is
$$\beta p_{1D}=\frac{\rho}{1-a\rho}=\sum_{j=1}^\infty a^{j-1}\rho^j,\qquad a\rho<1.$$
After the first $M\ge1$ terms, the exact nonnegative remainder (strictly positive when $a>0$) is $\rho(a\rho)^M/(1-a\rho)$, bounded by $\rho r^M/(1-r)$ whenever $a\rho\le r<1$. At fixed $\rho>0$ with $a\rho<1$, as $N,L\to\infty$ with $N/L=\rho$,
$$\lim\frac{\beta F}{N}=\log\!\left(\frac{\rho\lambda}{1-a\rho}\right)-1,$$
with finite-size excess between $0$ and $(1+\log N)/N$.
items.strategy:
1.1 The single-rod momentum Lebesgue integral is $\int_{\mathbb R}e^{-\beta p^2/(2m)}dp=\sqrt{2\pi m/\beta}$ by [F2] and [F8]. By [F5] and Tonelli [F6], the $N$ momentum factors integrate to the product of these integrals. Dividing by $h_0^N$ gives $\lambda^{-N}$. [given, F2, F5, F6, F8, algebra]

1.2 By [F2] and the bounded Riemann-to-Lebesgue agreement in [F8], each normalized scalar momentum Gaussian has second moment $m/\beta$. Thus the mean kinetic energy of each rod is $1/(2\beta)$ and the total mean is $U=N/(2\beta)$. [given, F2, F8, algebra]

1.3 The allowed labelled position set is a finite union of closed bounded ordering polytopes in $[a/2,L-a/2]^N$, hence compact by [F9]. Its boundary is contained in finitely many box faces and contact hyperplanes $x_i-x_j=\pm a$, each a compact graph over a coordinate rectangle, so [F7] makes it Jordan measurable. Fix one label ordering $\pi$ and sort its centers as $x_{\pi(1)}\le\cdots\le x_{\pi(N)}$. On that sector set $y_i=x_{\pi(i)}-a/2-(i-1)a$ and $\ell=L-Na>0$; the hard-core inequalities become the closed bounded, hence compact, ordered simplex $S_\ell:=\{0\le y_1\le\cdots\le y_N\le\ell\}$ by [F9]. Its boundary is contained in the box faces and finitely many tie hyperplanes, each a compact graph over a coordinate rectangle; [F7] therefore makes $S_\ell$ Jordan measurable. The affine permutation map has absolute determinant $1$, so [F3] preserves Jordan volume. The $N!$ coordinate permutations of $S_\ell$ partition $[0,\ell]^N$ up to the tie hyperplanes, which have content zero by [F7]; their equal volumes sum to $\ell^N$, hence each simplex has volume $\ell^N/N!$. The $N!$ labelled order sectors cover the allowed set and overlap only on the stated content-zero contact hyperplanes. Therefore its Jordan content is $\ell^N$, and [F5] gives the full labelled position Lebesgue measure $\ell^N$. [given, A1, F3, F5, F7, F9, algebra]

2.1 The reference measure divides the position-momentum integral by $N!h_0^N$. Product Lebesgue measure and Tonelli [F5, F6] separate the position measure $\ell^N$ from step 1.3 and the momentum integral from step 1.1. Thus $Z_N=\ell^N/(N!\lambda^N)$. [F1, F5, F6, step 1.1, step 1.3, algebra]

3.1 By the product, quotient and integer-power laws in [F4], $F=-\beta^{-1}[N\log((L-Na)/\lambda)-\log N!]$, using the logarithm derivative in [F4] at fixed $N,a,\beta$ gives $p_{1D}=N/[\beta(L-Na)]$. Substituting $\rho=N/L$ yields $\beta p_{1D}=\rho/(1-a\rho)$. [F1, F4, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 At $a=0$, the virial series has first term $\rho$ and all higher terms zero, so its remainder after any $M\ge1$ terms is zero. For $0\le a\rho<1$, the finite geometric identity $\sum_{j=1}^M(a\rho)^{j-1}=(1-(a\rho)^M)/(1-a\rho)$ gives the stated virial partial sum and exact remainder after multiplication by $\rho$. If $a\rho\le r<1$, then $(a\rho)^M/(1-a\rho)\le r^M/(1-r)$, proving the uniform bound. [step 3.1, algebra]

5.1 At fixed $\rho>0$, $L-Na=N(1/\rho-a)>0$, so the laws in [F4] give $$\frac{\beta F}{N}=-\log((L-Na)/\lambda)+\frac{\log N!}{N}.$$ For each integer $k=1,\ldots,N-1$, monotonicity of $\log$ bounds its integral on $[k,k+1]$ between $\log k$ and $\log(k+1)$. Summing gives $$\int_1^N\log x\,dx\le\log N!\le\int_1^N\log x\,dx+\log N.$$ For $N=1$ the sums and integral are empty and zero. Since [F4] gives $(x\log x-x)'=\log x$, the integral is $N\log N-N+1$. Hence $\log N!=N\log N-N+\epsilon_N$ with $1\le\epsilon_N\le1+\log N$. Substitution and [F4] cancel $\log N$, yielding $$\frac{\beta F}{N}=\log\!\left(\frac{\rho\lambda}{1-a\rho}\right)-1+\frac{\epsilon_N}{N}.$$ The excess is nonnegative and at most $(1+\log N)/N$. Finally, $\log N=\int_1^Ndx/x\le\int_1^Ndx/\sqrt{x}=2(\sqrt N-1)$, so that upper bound tends to zero and proves the stated thermodynamic limit. [F4, step 2.1, algebra] ∎

items.title: Finite spherical-shell gas and its exact marginal
items.design_state: Initial authoring complete; current prerequisite availability and readiness disposition are recorded in batch evidence.
items.statement:
Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ as defined in [[def-countable-choice]], the mathematical hypothesis required by the spherical-marginal supplier. Let $N,d\ge1$, $D=dN\ge2$, and let $B=\prod_{j=1}^d[0,L_j]\subset\mathbb R^d$ have side lengths $L_j>0$ in metres and volume $V=\prod_jL_j$ in $\mathrm m^d$. Let $m>0$ kg and $E>0$ joules, and set $R=\sqrt{2mE}$ in kg m s$^{-1}$. Take one operationally indistinguishable species of $N$ particles as specified by [[post-csm-counting-and-physical-observables]]. On the auxiliary labelled cover, take independent uniform positions $q_i\in B$ with density $V^{-1}$ and, independently, the momentum law
$$P=RZ/|Z|,$$
where $Z\in\mathbb R^D$ has the independent standard-normal coordinate law defined in [[thm-csm-examples-spherical-marginal]] and $P=0$ is assigned on the null event $Z=0$. This product law is invariant under particle permutations, so it defines the stated model preparation on the quotient; a one-particle marginal means the law of a uniformly selected particle. This is a specified spherical-shell preparation: $H(P)=|P|^2/(2m)=E$ almost surely, with no assumption about a trajectory or equilibration. For any momentum block of $k$ coordinates with $1\le k<D$, its density is $f_{D,k}$ from [[thm-csm-examples-spherical-marginal]]. In particular the total-energy variance is zero J$^2$.

Compare the separate canonical ideal-gas preparation of [[pthm-csm-ideal-gas-ensemble]] with the same $N,d,m,B$ and one-species convention, at $\beta=D/(2E)>0$. Its mean total energy is also $E$, but its variance is $D/(2\beta^2)>0$ J$^2$. If $N>1$, the uniformly selected particle's $d$-component shell marginal has compact support because $d<D$, whereas its canonical Gaussian momentum has positive probability outside every finite-radius ball. The two finite preparations therefore differ despite their matched mean energy. For $N=1$, the full momentum vector is singular on its sphere and the density formula for $k=D$ is not asserted.
items.strategy:
1.1 Under the shell preparation [F1] and its explicit law [A1], $|P|=R$ almost surely by the definition of $P$; hence $H(P)=R^2/(2m)=E$ on every realization outside the null event $Z=0$. A constant random variable has variance zero. [given, F1, A1, algebra]



2.1 For $1\le k<D$, the first $k$ momentum coordinates are the projection in [F2], so their exact Lebesgue density is the displayed $f_{D,k}$ with support in $|p|\le R$. Its boundary may carry no atom; the underlying Gaussian direction has a density and $Z=0$ is null. [F2, step 1.1]



2.2 Choose $\beta=D/(2E)$. By [F3], the canonical mean energy is $D/(2\beta)=E$ and its variance is $D/(2\beta^2)>0$. Thus it cannot have the shell law of step 1.1, whose energy variance is zero. [given, F3, step 1.1, algebra]



3.1 If $N>1$, then $d<D$ and [F2] gives the one-particle momentum block a density supported in the radius-$R$ ball. By [F3], its canonical Gaussian has strictly positive density at every point of $\mathbb R^d$, so its integral over, for example, the open annulus $R<|p|<2R$ is positive, while the shell probability of that annulus is zero. Therefore the one-particle marginals differ as well. For $N=1$, $d=D$ and the full shell law is singular, so no $k=D$ density assertion has been used. [F2, F3, step 2.1] ∎

David Tong, Statistical Physics, §2.2, canonical ideal-gas momentum distribution

items.title: Unpinned translation zero-mode divergence
items.design_state: Initial authoring complete; current prerequisite availability and readiness disposition are recorded in batch evidence.
items.statement:
Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ as defined in [[def-countable-choice]] for the Euclidean Lebesgue measure of the phase-space boxes below. Take $N\ge3$ resolved displacement coordinates $q_i\in\mathbb R$ in metres and momenta $p_i\in\mathbb R$ in kg m s$^{-1}$ on a periodic chain, with $q_{N+1}=q_1$, mass $m>0$ kg, spring stiffness $\kappa>0$ in J m$^{-2}$, and
$$H(q,p)=\sum_{i=1}^N\frac{p_i^2}{2m}+\frac{\kappa}{2}\sum_{i=1}^N(q_{i+1}-q_i)^2.$$
Adopt inverse temperature $\beta>0$ in J$^{-1}$ and fixed action reference $h_0=a_0>0$ in J s under [[post-csm-examples-ensemble-preparations]]. Because the coordinates are resolved, use the reference $dq\,dp/h_0^N$ with no particle-exchange factorial. Define the partition integral
$$Z:=\int_{\mathbb R^N\times\mathbb R^N}\exp(-\beta H(q,p))\,\frac{dq\,dp}{h_0^N},$$
where $\exp$ is the real exponential of [[def-real-exponential-function-and-e]]. The unpinned position integral is infinite, so this model has no normalized canonical probability on the full position space.
items.strategy:
1.1 Put $r_1:=0$ and use coordinates $u:=q_1$, $r_i:=q_i-q_1$ for $2\le i\le N$. The linear bijection $(u,r_2,\ldots,r_N)\mapsto(q_1,\ldots,q_N)=(u,u+r_2,\ldots,u+r_N)$ has determinant $1$. With $r_{N+1}:=r_1$, every periodic difference satisfies $q_{i+1}-q_i=r_{i+1}-r_i$, so the potential is independent of $u$; the momentum term is also independent of $u$. On each compact coordinate box the change-of-variables supplier [F3] therefore gives the phase-volume Jacobian $1$. [given, A1, F3, algebra]



2.1 Under the declared reference convention [F1], choose any compact coordinate box $C$ of positive volume in $(r_2,\ldots,r_N,p)$. The Hamiltonian is continuous and hence bounded above on $C$ by a finite $H_C$ by [F4]. By [F2], $C$ has Lebesgue measure $\operatorname{vol}(C)$. On $u\in[-R,R]$ and $(r,p)\in C$, the integrand is at least $e^{-\beta H_C}$; the determinant-one map in step 1.1 and [F2] show this slab contributes at least $2R e^{-\beta H_C}\operatorname{vol}(C)/h_0^N$ to the partition integral by [F5]. This lower bound is unbounded as $R\to\infty$, so $Z=\infty$ and no normalization exists. [F1, F2, F4, F5, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

items.title: Maxwell speed marginal and Poisson number example
items.design_state: Initial authoring complete; current prerequisite availability and readiness disposition are recorded in batch evidence.
items.statement:
Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ as required by [[pthm-csm-ideal-gas-ensemble]]. In a canonical sector $N\ge1$ of the massive $d=3$ ideal-gas model of one operationally indistinguishable species, choose any mass $m>0$ in kg and inverse temperature $\beta>0$ in J$^{-1}$. The most probable speed of a uniformly selected particle is $\sqrt{2/(m\beta)}$ and its ensemble mean speed is $\sqrt{8/(\pi m\beta)}$. In the separate grand model, which includes the vacuum sector, choose the chemical potential
$$\mu_{\rm chem}=\beta^{-1}\log(\lambda^3/V),$$
so the mean activity parameter $\nu=\exp(\beta\mu_{\rm chem})V/\lambda^3$ equals $1$, where $V$ is in m$^3$, $\lambda$ in metres, and $\mu_{\rm chem}$ in joules. The particle count then has the Poisson$(1)$ law, including $\mathbb P(N=0)=\mathbb P(N=1)=\exp(-1)$.
items.strategy:
1.1 Specializing the $d=3$ clauses of [F1] gives the stated mode and mean of the model speed distribution; these are distributional functionals, not values assigned to every individual particle. [F1]

2.1 Substituting [A1] and applying [F2] gives $\exp(\beta\mu_{\rm chem})=\lambda^3/V$, hence $\nu=1$ in [F1]. The Poisson formula then gives $\mathbb P(N=j)=\exp(-1)/j!$, so the $j=0$ and $j=1$ probabilities both equal $\exp(-1)$. [A1, F1, F2, algebra] ∎

items.title: Exact finite-ring correlations and limiting correlation length at a chosen coupling
items.design_state: Initial authoring complete; current prerequisite availability and readiness disposition are recorded in batch evidence.
items.statement:
For any finite $N\ge2$ at zero field, choose coupling $J>0$ in joules and inverse temperature $\beta=(\log2)/(2J)$ in J$^{-1}$. Then $t=\tanh(\beta J)=1/3$ and the exact ring correlation at separation $1\le r<N$ is
$$\mathbb E_N[s_i s_{i+r}]=\frac{3^{-r}+3^{-(N-r)}}{1+3^{-N}}.$$
At fixed $r$, the limit is $3^{-r}=e^{-r\log3}$, so the correlation length is $1/\log3$ lattice spacings.
items.strategy:
1.1 Since $\tanh(x)=(e^{2x}-1)/(e^{2x}+1)$, the choice [A1] gives $t=(2-1)/(2+1)=1/3$. [A1, algebra]



2.1 Substituting $t=1/3$ in [F1] gives the displayed finite-$N$ correlation. Its fixed-$r$ limit is $3^{-r}$ by the theorem's error bound, and $3^{-r}=e^{-r\log3}$ gives $\xi=1/\log3$. [F1, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ as required by [[pthm-csm-spherical-shell-gas]], and use its one-species rectangular-box model. Take $d=3$, $N=2$, $D=6$, mass $m>0$ in kg, and energy $E>0$ in joules, so the momentum radius is $R=\sqrt{2mE}$ in kg m s$^{-1}$. A uniformly selected particle's three-momentum block ($k=3$) under the shell preparation has density
$$f_{6,3}(p)=\frac{4}{\pi^2R^3}\sqrt{1-\frac{|p|^2}{R^2}},\qquad |p|<R,$$
and zero for $|p|\ge R$. A canonical ideal gas with $\beta=D/(2E)=3/E$ in J$^{-1}$ has the same mean total energy but assigns positive probability to the annulus $R<|p_\star|<2R$ for the uniformly selected particle's momentum $p_\star$.
items.strategy:
1.1 Substituting $D=6,k=3$ into [F1] gives exponent $(6-3-2)/2=1/2$ and coefficient $\Gamma(3)/[\Gamma(3/2)(\pi R^2)^{3/2}]=4/(\pi^2R^3)$ using $\Gamma(3)=2$ and $\Gamma(3/2)=\sqrt\pi/2$. This is the displayed density. [A1, F1, algebra]

2.1 The shell block has probability zero outside the radius-$R$ ball by [F1]. The canonical Gaussian vector density from [F2] is positive throughout the nonempty annulus $R<|p|<2R$, which has positive volume, so that event has positive canonical probability. Therefore the two finite momentum marginals differ. [F1, F2, step 1.1] ∎

row.title: Finite Bernoulli fluctuations and matching exponential rates

items.design_state: Local mathematical definition added on the A page because the inspected finite probability suppliers define expectation but not variance; sourced to Zhao, §4.1, Definition 4.1.
items.statement:
Let $(\Omega,w)$ be a finite probability space: $\Omega$ is a finite set, each weight $w(\omega)$ is nonnegative, and $\sum_{\omega\in\Omega}w(\omega)=1$. Let $X:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ be a real random variable and let $\mathbb E[X]=\sum_{\omega\in\Omega}X(\omega)w(\omega)$. Its **variance** is

$$\operatorname{Var}(X):=\mathbb E[(X-\mathbb E[X])^2]=\sum_{\omega\in\Omega}(X(\omega)-\mathbb E[X])^2w(\omega).$$

All sums are finite, so the definition requires no additional integrability or moment hypothesis.
items.strategy: Definition only; finite expectations are the finite weighted sums supplied by its explicit dependency.
items.title: Variance of a finite real random variable

references.title: Y. Zhao, MIT 18.218 Probabilistic Method in Combinatorics, §4.1, Definition 4.1

items.design_state: Complete conditional carrier; exact source interfaces and readiness disposition are recorded in batch-35 evidence.
items.statement:
Let $n\ge1$ be an integer, let $p\in(0,1)$, and give $\Omega_n=\{0,1\}^n$ the explicitly stipulated product probability whose singleton weights are
$$P_p(\{(x_1,\ldots,x_n)\})=\prod_{i=1}^n p^{x_i}(1-p)^{1-x_i};$$
for an event $A\subseteq\Omega_n$, $P_p(A)$ is the sum of these weights over $x\in A$.
Write $X_i(x)=x_i$, $K=\sum_{i=1}^nX_i$, and $\overline X=K/n$. These variables and all probabilities are dimensionless. The product law is an adopted sampling model; independence is an assumption of that law, not an inference about any apparatus or equilibrium system.

For $a\in(0,1)$ define the Bernoulli relative-entropy rate
$$D(a\Vert p)=a\log\frac ap+(1-a)\log\frac{1-a}{1-p},$$
and set $D(0\Vert p)=-\log(1-p)$ and $D(1\Vert p)=-\log p$. Then
$$\mathbb E K=np,\qquad \operatorname{Var}(K)=np(1-p),$$
and for every dimensionless $\varepsilon>0$,
$$P_p\bigl(|\overline X-p|\ge\varepsilon\bigr)\le\frac{p(1-p)}{n\varepsilon^2},\qquad P_p\bigl(|\overline X-p|\ge\varepsilon\bigr)\le 2e^{-2n\varepsilon^2}.$$
For $p<a<1$ and $0<a<p$, respectively,
$$P_p(K\ge na)\le e^{-nD(a\Vert p)},\qquad P_p(K\le na)\le e^{-nD(a\Vert p)}.$$
For each integer $0\le k\le n$, putting $a=k/n$ gives the point-mass bounds
$$\frac1{n+1}e^{-nD(a\Vert p)}\le P_p(K=k)\le e^{-nD(a\Vert p)}.$$
Consequently, for every sequence of integers $k_n\in\{0,\ldots,n\}$ with $k_n/n\to a\in(0,1)$,
$$\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac1n\log P_p(K=k_n)=-D(a\Vert p).$$
All conclusions are conditional calculations for this finite product model and make no claim that physical outcomes are independent or that a small model probability is a logical contradiction.
items.strategy:
**Given:** The finite IID Bernoulli model and all hypotheses in the Statement.

1.1 The total weight is $\prod_{i=1}^n(p+(1-p))=1$, so the stipulated weights form a finite probability law. Summing over all coordinates except $i$ gives $P(X_i=1)=p$ and $P(X_i=0)=1-p$; the product factorization also gives independence. For $0\le k\le n$ put $c_{n,k}:=\#\{S\subseteq\{1,\ldots,n\}:|S|=k\}$. The set of coordinates with value $1$ gives a bijection between outcomes with $K=k$ and such subsets, so $P(K=k)=c_{n,k}p^k(1-p)^{n-k}$. By [F4] and [F12], $\mathbb E X_i=p$ and $\operatorname{Var}(X_i)=\mathbb E[(X_i-p)^2]=p(1-p)$. For $i\ne j$, the product weights factor the finite sum, giving $\mathbb E[(X_i-p)(X_j-p)]=\mathbb E(X_i-p)\mathbb E(X_j-p)=0$. Expanding $K$ and $(K-np)^2$ therefore yields $\mathbb E K=np$ and $\operatorname{Var}(K)=np(1-p)$. [given, F1, F2, F3, F4, F12, algebra]

1.2 The finite-sum definition [F5] and product weights give $$M_K(s)=\sum_{x\in\Omega_n}P_p(x)e^{s\sum_i x_i}=\prod_{i=1}^n\bigl((1-p)+pe^s\bigr)=(1-p+pe^s)^n.$$ This is a finite factorization, so no limiting interchange is involved. [given, F5, F6, algebra]

1.3 On $0<a<1$, differentiating the displayed expression for $D$ with [F9] gives $D(p\Vert p)=0$, $\partial_aD(a\Vert p)|_{a=p}=0$, and $\partial_a^2D(a\Vert p)=1/[a(1-a)]\ge4$, since $a(1-a)\le1/4$. Let $G(a)=D(a\Vert p)-2(a-p)^2$. Then $G(p)=G'(p)=0$ and $G''\ge0$. For $a>p$, the mean value theorem applied first to $G'$ and then to $G$ gives $G'(a)\ge0$ and $G(a)\ge0$; for $a<p$, the same two applications give $G'(a)\le0$ and again $G(a)\ge0$. Thus $D(a\Vert p)\ge2(a-p)^2$ for interior $a$. At $a\downarrow0$, the only noncontinuous-looking term is $a\log a=-\log(1/a)/(1/a)$, which tends to zero by [F11]; at $a\uparrow1$ the analogous term is $(1-a)\log(1-a)$. The remaining factors are continuous, so the endpoint extensions preserve the inequality. [given, F7, F8, F9, F10, F11, algebra]

2.1 Fix $1\le k\le n-1$ and let $a=k/n$. For $0\le j\le n$ put $q_j=c_{n,j}a^j(1-a)^{n-j}$. These are the count probabilities under the finite product weights with parameter $a$; their sum is $1$ by factoring the total weight as $(a+(1-a))^n$. For each $0\le j<n$, count pairs $(S,T)$ with $S\subset T\subseteq\{1,\ldots,n\}$, $|S|=j$, and $|T|=j+1$. Choosing $S$ first gives $c_{n,j}(n-j)$ pairs, while choosing $T$ first gives $c_{n,j+1}(j+1)$; hence $c_{n,j+1}/c_{n,j}=(n-j)/(j+1)$. Therefore $$\frac{q_{j+1}}{q_j}=\frac{n-j}{j+1}\frac{a}{1-a}.$$ The factor $(n-j)/(j+1)$ decreases strictly with $j$, since $(n-j-1)(j+1)<(n-j)(j+2)$ for $j<n-1$. At $j=k-1$ the ratio is $(n-k+1)/(n-k)>1$, and at $j=k$ it is $k/(k+1)<1$. Thus the sequence increases through $q_k$ and decreases after it, so $q_k$ is the largest of its $n+1$ masses. Their sum is $1$, whence $1/(n+1)\le q_k\le1$. [given, step 1.1, algebra]

2.2 Pointwise on $\Omega_n$, $\mathbf 1_{\{|\overline X-p|\ge\varepsilon\}}\le (\overline X-p)^2/\varepsilon^2$. Summing this inequality with the finite weights and using step 1.1 gives the first probability bound. [given, F4, step 1.1, algebra]

2.3 Suppose first $p<a<1$ and put $s=\log\!\bigl(a(1-p)/(p(1-a))\bigr)>0$. On $\{K\ge na\}$, $e^{sK}\ge e^{sna}$, so the finite expectation of the nonnegative random variable $e^{sK}$ is at least $e^{sna}P_p(K\ge na)$. By step 1.2, $$P_p(K\ge na)\le e^{-sna}(1-p+pe^s)^n=e^{-nD(a\Vert p)},$$ where $e^s=a(1-p)/(p(1-a))$, $1-p+pe^s=(1-p)/(1-a)$, and [F7]–[F8] simplify the logarithm. If $0<a<p$, the same value of $s$ is negative; on $\{K\le na\}$ one again has $e^{sK}\ge e^{sna}$, and the same substitution yields $P_p(K\le na)\le e^{-nD(a\Vert p)}$. This proves both exponential tail bounds without using a general concentration theorem as a premise. [given, F4, F5, F6, F7, F8, step 1.2, algebra]

3.1 Direct division of the two point probabilities, using the same subset count $c_{n,k}$ from step 1.1, gives $$\frac{P_p(K=k)}{q_k}=\left(\frac pa\right)^k\left(\frac{1-p}{1-a}\right)^{n-k}.$$ Since $k=na$ and $n-k=n(1-a)$, [F7]–[F8] give the logarithm of this ratio as $n a\log(p/a)+n(1-a)\log((1-p)/(1-a))=-nD(a\Vert p)$, so the ratio is $e^{-nD(a\Vert p)}$. Combining with step 2.1 proves the claimed bounds for $1\le k\le n-1$. For $k=0$ and $k=n$, direct evaluation gives $P_p(K=0)=(1-p)^n=e^{-nD(0\Vert p)}$ and $P_p(K=n)=p^n=e^{-nD(1\Vert p)}$, which satisfy the same inequalities. [given, F7, F8, step 1.1, step 2.1, algebra]

3.2 If $0<\varepsilon<1$, split the deviation event into the upper threshold $a_+=p+\varepsilon$ and lower threshold $a_-=p-\varepsilon$. For an interior threshold apply step 2.3 and then step 1.3; at $a_+=1$ or $a_-=0$ use the exact endpoint probability $p^n$ or $(1-p)^n$ and the endpoint case of step 1.3; a threshold outside $[0,1]$ gives an empty event. Each nonempty tail is at most $e^{-2n\varepsilon^2}$, so their sum is at most $2e^{-2n\varepsilon^2}$. If $\varepsilon\ge1$, the deviation event is empty because $0\le\overline X\le1$ and $0<p<1$. [given, step 2.3, step 1.3, algebra]

4.1 If $k_n/n\to a\in(0,1)$, then $D(k_n/n\Vert p)\to D(a\Vert p)$ by continuity on $(0,1)$. Taking logarithms of step 3.1 and dividing by $n$ bounds $n^{-1}\log P_p(K=k_n)$ between $-D(k_n/n\Vert p)-\log(n+1)/n$ and $-D(k_n/n\Vert p)$. By [F11], $\log(n+1)/n\to0$, so the squeeze theorem gives the stated rate. These probabilities remain conditional on the explicitly stipulated product law; no finite sample or measurement is asserted. [given, F7, F11, step 3.1] ∎

items.statement:
Fix $N\ge1$ and $\epsilon>0$ joules. Let $\Omega_N=A_N\sqcup B_N\sqcup C_N$ be disjoint finite sectors with $|A_N|=1$, $|B_N|=1$, and $|C_N|=4^N$, and define the energy $H_N$ to be $0$, $N\epsilon$, and $2N\epsilon$ on those sectors, respectively. The model is global and size-dependent. Here *product-additive* means that one fixed finite one-site alphabet $\Gamma$ supplies $\Omega_N=\Gamma^N$ for every $N$, and one fixed one-site energy function $h:\Gamma\to\mathbb R$ (with values measured in joules) satisfies $H_N(\gamma_1,\ldots,\gamma_N)=\sum_{i=1}^Nh(\gamma_i)$. The present family is non-product-additive; no local, short-range, or fluid interpretation is assumed.

Use counting measure on each $\Omega_N$ as the reference measure, so every individual state has weight one. For a real inverse-energy parameter $\beta$ in joules$^{-1}$, define the finite exponential-tilt probability by
$$Z_N(\beta)=\sum_{\omega\in\Omega_N}e^{-\beta H_N(\omega)}=1+e^{-\beta N\epsilon}+4^Ne^{-2\beta N\epsilon},\qquad P_{\beta,N}(\omega)=\frac{e^{-\beta H_N(\omega)}}{Z_N(\beta)}.$$
For $\beta>0$ this is the adopted canonical preparation. For $\beta\le0$ it is only the same finite counting formula used algebraically; no negative-temperature reservoir is asserted. Also, for a shell half-width $\Delta$ in joules with $0\le\Delta<N\epsilon$, define $\mathcal S_{N,\Delta}=\{\omega:|H_N(\omega)-N\epsilon|\le\Delta\}$ and give it the uniform counting probability $Q_{N,\Delta}(\omega)=|\mathcal S_{N,\Delta}|^{-1}$ for $\omega\in\mathcal S_{N,\Delta}$.

For every real $\beta$, the finite exponential-tilt probability of $B_N$ obeys
$$P_{\beta,N}(B_N)\le\frac{1}{2^{N+1}+1},$$
whereas the shell probability of $B_N$ is $1$. Define the dimensionless normalized log partition function $\psi_N(\beta)=N^{-1}\log Z_N(\beta)$. Then
$$\psi_N(\beta)\longrightarrow\psi(\beta):=\max\{0,\log4-2\beta\epsilon\},\qquad 0\le\psi_N(\beta)-\psi(\beta)\le\frac{\log3}{N}.$$
For $\beta>0$, define the canonical mean energy per member by $u_N(\beta):=N^{-1}\mathbb E_{P_{\beta,N}}[H_N]$ and, when the limit exists, set $u(\beta):=\lim_{N\to\infty}u_N(\beta)$. The corner occurs at the positive inverse temperature $\beta_c=(\log2)/\epsilon$. The limit $u(\beta)$ exists for every $\beta>0$ and equals $2\epsilon$ for $0<\beta<\beta_c$, $\epsilon$ at $\beta=\beta_c$, and $0$ for $\beta>\beta_c$. In this item, a **first-order transition point** means a positive-$\beta$ point where $u$ has finite but unequal one-sided limits; thus the jump at $\beta_c$ is first order under this explicit convention. Every finite-$N$ function $\psi_N$ is real analytic. This is one explicit global finite-state countermodel, not a universal criterion for phase transitions or ensemble equivalence in short-range matter.
items.strategy:
**Given:** The exact model data and law in the Statement; $\beta$ is positive for the canonical physical interpretation and may be any real number in the separate finite algebraic claims.

1.1 If this family were product-additive under the definition in the Statement, its fixed alphabet would have $|\Gamma|=|\Omega_1|=6$, forcing $|\Omega_2|=|\Gamma|^2=36$. But $|\Omega_2|=1+1+4^2=18$. Thus no such product decomposition exists. The three sector weights in the finite exponential tilt are $1$, $x$, and $4^Nx^2$, where $x=e^{-\beta N\epsilon}>0$; they sum to the displayed positive finite $Z_N(\beta)$, so division by $Z_N$ gives a finite probability law as in [F10]. For $\beta>0$, [A1] and [F1] identify this normalized counting weight with the adopted canonical branch; for $\beta\le0$ it remains only the stated algebraic expression. [given, A1, F1, F10, algebra]

1.2 The energies of $A_N$ and $C_N$ differ from $N\epsilon$ by exactly $N\epsilon$. The condition $\Delta<N\epsilon$ excludes both sectors from $\mathcal S_{N,\Delta}$, while $B_N\subseteq\mathcal S_{N,\Delta}$. Thus the shell is exactly the one-state set $B_N$ and its uniform counting probability assigns $B_N$ probability one. [given, A2, algebra]

1.3 Put $M_N=\max\{1,4^Nx^2\}$. If $x\le1$, then $x\le M_N$; if $x>1$, then $4^Nx^2\ge x$ since $N\ge1$. Hence $M_N\le Z_N\le3M_N$. By [F2]–[F3], $$\frac1N\log M_N=\max\{0,\log4-2\beta\epsilon\}=\psi(\beta),$$ so taking logarithms in $M_N\le Z_N\le3M_N$ gives $0\le\psi_N-\psi\le(\log3)/N$, and consequently $\psi_N\to\psi$. [given, F2, F3, algebra]

1.4 By [F4], $\exp$ is a power series converging for every real argument, so [F6] makes $\exp$ real analytic on $\mathbb R$. The affine polynomial $\beta\mapsto-\beta N\epsilon$ is real analytic, hence [F7] makes $\beta\mapsto e^{-\beta N\epsilon}$ real analytic as well. [given, F4, F6, F7, algebra]

2.1 Since $(1-2^Nx)^2\ge0$, $1+4^Nx^2\ge2^{N+1}x$. Therefore $Z_N=1+x+4^Nx^2\ge(2^{N+1}+1)x$, and division by $Z_N>0$ gives $P_{\beta,N}(B_N)\le(2^{N+1}+1)^{-1}$. [given, F10, step 1.1, algebra]

2.2 The equality $\log4=2\log2$ from [F3] gives the unique corner $\beta_c=(\log2)/\epsilon>0$. On $0<\beta<\beta_c$, the larger branch is $\log4-2\beta\epsilon$ and has slope $-2\epsilon$; on $\beta>\beta_c$ the larger branch is $0$ and has slope $0$. The one-sided slopes differ. [given, F2, F3, step 1.3, algebra]

2.3 The exponential is positive, so $Z_N=1+e^{-\beta N\epsilon}+4^Ne^{-2\beta N\epsilon}>0$ for every real $\beta$. Its expression as a sum and product of the analytic function in step 1.4 is real analytic by [F7]. [given, F2, F7, step 1.4, algebra]

3.1 By [F12], with [F11] identifying $H_N$ as a finite real random variable, the mean energy per member is $u_N(\beta)=\epsilon\bigl(x+2\cdot4^Nx^2\bigr)/Z_N$ for $\beta>0$. If $0<\beta<\beta_c$, divide numerator and denominator by the high-sector weight $4^Nx^2$: the low-to-high ratio is $e^{-N(\log4-2\beta\epsilon)}\to0$ and the middle-to-high ratio is $e^{N(\beta\epsilon-\log4)}\le2^{-N}\to0$, so $u_N(\beta)\to2\epsilon$. If $\beta>\beta_c$, both non-low weights $x=e^{-\beta N\epsilon}$ and $4^Nx^2=e^{N(\log4-2\beta\epsilon)}$ tend to zero, so $u_N(\beta)\to0$. At $\beta=\beta_c$, the three sector weights are $1$, $2^{-N}$, and $1$, so $u_N(\beta_c)=\epsilon(2^{-N}+2)/(2+2^{-N})\to\epsilon$. These limits give the stated piecewise $u$ and its unequal one-sided limits. [given, F11, F12, step 2.2, algebra]

3.2 Fix $\beta_0\in\mathbb R$ and put $z_0=Z_N(\beta_0)>0$. By step 1.4, $\exp$ is real analytic; [F9] gives $\exp'(\log z_0)=z_0\ne0$, so [F8] gives a real-analytic local inverse near $z_0$. By the inverse definition [F2], that local inverse is $\log$ on this neighborhood, hence $\log$ is real analytic near $z_0$. [given, F2, F8, F9, step 1.4, step 2.3, algebra]

4.1 By [F5] the target property is real analyticity, and [F7] makes the composition $N^{-1}\log Z_N$ real analytic using steps 2.3 and 3.2. Hence every finite-$N$ function $\psi_N$ is real analytic. The derivative jump in step 2.2 belongs to the limiting function, not to a finite-$N$ singularity. [given, F5, F7, step 2.2, step 2.3, step 3.2, algebra] ∎

items.statement:
Assume the Axiom of Choice. The following are separate calculations for three explicitly defined models.

**Diffusive-scale walk.** Let $D>0$ have units m$^2$s$^{-1}$, fix $t\ge0$ seconds, and let $(\delta t_j)_{j\ge1}$ be any positive sequence tending to zero, with $\ell_j=\sqrt{2D\delta t_j}$ metres and $n_j=\lfloor t/\delta t_j\rfloor$. For each $j$, on the finite product space $\Omega_j=\{-1,1\}^{n_j}$ with uniform probability, let $\Xi_i$ be the coordinate increments and
$$S_j=\ell_j\sum_{i=1}^{n_j}\Xi_i.$$
For the dimensionless lattice index $r\in\mathbb Z$, define
$$u_n(r):=2^{-n}\#\{(x_1,\ldots,x_n)\in\{-1,1\}^n:\sum_{i=1}^n x_i=r\},$$
with the empty sum equal to zero. Then $\mathbb E S_j=0$, $\operatorname{Var}(S_j)=n_j\ell_j^2$, and the lattice probabilities satisfy $u_{n+1}(r)=\tfrac12u_n(r-1)+\tfrac12u_n(r+1)$ with $u_0(r)=\mathbf1_{\{r=0\}}$. For every wave number $k\in\mathbb R$ in m$^{-1}$,
$$\varphi_{S_j}(k)=\cos(\ell_j k)^{n_j}.$$
The laws of $S_j$ converge weakly on $\mathbb R$ to $N(0,2Dt)$, the normal probability law with mean zero and variance $2Dt$ (in m$^2$). The conclusion is fixed-time marginal convergence only.

**Periodic rotor.** Let $\mathbb T:=\mathbb R/(2\pi\mathbb Z)$ with its quotient topology, and let the phase space $\mathcal X=\mathbb T\times\mathbb R$ have its metrizable product topology. Let $q\in\mathbb T$ be a dimensionless angle, $p\in\mathbb R$ have units kg m$^2$s$^{-1}$, and $I>0$ have units kg m$^2$. Define the model energy $H(q,p)=p^2/(2I)$ and, for time $s\in\mathbb R$ measured in seconds, the flow
$$\Phi_s(q,p)=\bigl(q+ps/I\ {\rm mod}\ 2\pi,\ p\bigr).$$
For each $p_0\ne0$, the orbit is periodic with period $T=2\pi I/|p_0|$ seconds. Let $\nu$ be normalized arc length on $\mathbb T$, define the continuous inclusion $\iota_{p_0}(q)=(q,p_0)$, and for each Borel $E\subseteq\mathcal X$ set $\mu_0(E)=\nu(\iota_{p_0}^{-1}(E))$. Thus $\mu_0$ is the uniform angle probability on the fixed-$p_0$ orbit. For this invariant probability, *mixing* means $\mu_0(B\cap\Phi_s^{-1}C)\to\mu_0(B)\mu_0(C)$ for all Borel $B,C\subseteq\mathcal X$ as $s\to\infty$. The rotor is not mixing: for the half-circle arc $A=\{([q],p_0):q\in[0,\pi)\}$, where $[q]=q+2\pi\mathbb Z\in\mathbb T$, the mixing correlation fails along times $s=mT$ with positive integers $m$. For any $q_0=[\theta_0]\in\mathbb T$, the point-supported initial law $\delta_{(q_0,p_0)}$ (unit mass at $(q_0,p_0)$) has no weak limit as $s\to\infty$; the bounded continuous witness $g([\theta],p)=\cos(\theta-\theta_0)$ is well-defined because cosine is $2\pi$-periodic.

**Finite coarse-entropy model.** Let $\Omega=\{0,1,2,3\}$ with uniform reference probability and permutation $\mathcal T(0)=1,\mathcal T(1)=2,\mathcal T(2)=3,\mathcal T(3)=0$. Start from $\pi_0=(1/2,1/2,0,0)$, and evolve by pushforward under $\mathcal T$. For the coarse partition $\{\{0,1\},\{2,3\}\}$, let $(r_1,r_2)$ be any probability vector with $r_i\ge0$ and $r_1+r_2=1$, and define its coarse Shannon entropy by $H_c(r_1,r_2)=-\sum_{i:r_i>0}r_i\log r_i$ in nats. Define fine entropy analogously for a probability vector on the four states, using $0\log0=0$. The coarse entropies at times $0,1,2$ are $0,\log2,0$, while the fine entropy is $\log2$ at all three times. Thus deterministic invertibility and preservation of the uniform reference measure do not imply monotone coarse entropy.

The smooth-flow result [[thm-csm-examples-flow-fine-entropy]] has different hypotheses: it concerns positive $C^1$ densities on a flat torus transported by supplied jointly $C^2$ volume-preserving diffeomorphisms and preserves their dimensionless fine differential entropy. It supplies no monotonicity conclusion for coarse entropy in a finite permutation. These models report no observations and prove no diffusion limit from deterministic collisions.
items.strategy:
**Given:** The definitions and model assumptions in the Statement and Facts & Assumptions; assume full AC for the weak-convergence and normal-law suppliers.

1.1 Under the product-preparation convention [F1], for a fixed $j$ the uniform weight on $\{-1,1\}^{n_j}$ is a probability law, including the singleton case $n_j=0$. Each increment has mean zero and square one by [F2]–[F4]. Independence follows from the product weights, so the cross terms in $\mathbb E(\sum_i\Xi_i)^2$ vanish; hence $\mathbb E S_j=0$ and, by [F19], $\operatorname{Var}(S_j)=n_j\ell_j^2$. Conditioning on the last increment gives $u_{n+1}(r)=\tfrac12u_n(r-1)+\tfrac12u_n(r+1)$, with the stated initial mass. [given, A1, F1, F2, F3, F4, F19, algebra]

1.2 For the rotor, write $R_s(q)=q+p_0s/I$ modulo $2\pi$. At $T=2\pi I/|p_0|$, the angle increment is $2\pi$ when $p_0>0$ and $-2\pi$ when $p_0<0$, so $R_T$ is the identity. The stated full AC includes the countable-choice assumption of [F16]. For every Borel $E\subseteq\mathcal X$, $\iota_{p_0}^{-1}(\Phi_s^{-1}E)=R_s^{-1}(\iota_{p_0}^{-1}E)$; translation invariance in [F16] therefore gives $\mu_0(\Phi_s^{-1}E)=\mu_0(E)$, and in particular $\mu_0$ is invariant under the rotor flow. [given, A2, F9, F16, algebra]

1.3 Under the four-state pushforward, the first three probability vectors are $$\pi_0=(1/2,1/2,0,0),\quad \pi_1=(0,1/2,1/2,0),\quad \pi_2=(0,0,1/2,1/2).$$ The map $\mathcal T$ is a permutation, so it maps the uniform reference weights $1/4$ to themselves; it also leaves the multiset of the evolving fine probabilities unchanged, and each fine entropy is $-\tfrac12\log\tfrac12-\tfrac12\log\tfrac12=\log2$. The coarse cell probabilities for $\{\{0,1\},\{2,3\}\}$ are $(1,0)$, $(1/2,1/2)$, and $(0,1)$, giving coarse entropies $0,\log2,0$ under the zero-term convention. This proves the stated decrease. [given, A3, F11, algebra]

2.1 By independence and [F5], the characteristic function is $$\varphi_{S_j}(k)=\prod_{i=1}^{n_j}\mathbb E(e^{ik\ell_j\Xi_i})=\cos(\ell_j k)^{n_j}.$$ Fix $k$. Continuity of cosine and $\cos0=1$ make $\cos u>0$ for all sufficiently small $|u|$. For such $u$, put $f(u)=\log\cos u$. By the chain rule, $f'(u)=-\sin u/\cos u$ and $f'(0)=0$. From [F10], $\sin u/u\to\sin'(0)=1$ and $\cos u\to1$, so the difference quotient $f'(u)/u=-\sin u/(u\cos u)$ tends to $-1$; hence $f''(0)=-1$. The same derivative rules make $f$ twice differentiable on a neighbourhood of zero, so [F15] gives $\log\cos u=-u^2/2+o(u^2)$. For $t>0$, $n_j\delta t_j\to t$ because $0\le t-n_j\delta t_j<\delta t_j$, and therefore $$n_j\log\cos(\ell_jk)=-\frac{n_j\ell_j^2k^2}{2}+n_j\,o(\ell_j^2)\longrightarrow-Dtk^2.$$ Indeed $n_j\ell_j^2=2D n_j\delta t_j\to2Dt$, so $n_j\ell_j^2$ is bounded, while $o(\ell_j^2)/\ell_j^2\to0$; their product proves the remainder tends to zero. For $t=0$, $n_j=0$ and every law is $\delta_0$. Thus in all cases $\varphi_{S_j}(k)\to e^{-Dtk^2}=\varphi_{N(0,2Dt)}(k)$ for every real $k$, using [F6]–[F7] for the target law. [given, A1, F5, F6, F7, F10, F11, F12, F13, F14, F15, step 1.1, algebra]

2.2 The measure definition gives $\mu_0(A)=\nu([0,\pi))=1/2$. At each $s=mT$, $\Phi_s$ is the identity on the support of $\mu_0$, so $\mu_0(A\cap\Phi_s^{-1}A)=1/2\ne1/4=\mu_0(A)^2$, contradicting the mixing condition stated in the Statement. For $q_0=[\theta_0]$, the function $g([\theta],p)=\cos(\theta-\theta_0)$ is well-defined and continuous on the quotient because cosine is continuous and $2\pi$-periodic, and it is bounded by $1$. Its values are $1$ at times $mT$ and $-1$ at times $mT+T/2$, so its expectation has no limit. By [F18], weak convergence would force convergence of this expectation, so the evolving point laws have no weak limit. [given, F16, F18, step 1.2, algebra]

2.3 The mathematical result [F17] assumes a smooth diffeomorphic flow on a flat torus, divergence-free velocity, and a positive bounded $C^1$ density. The atomic four-state law in step 1.3 is not such a density or flow; its coarse-entropy decrease neither invokes nor contradicts that fine differential-entropy result. It establishes no monotonicity law for other coarse-graining procedures. [given, F17, step 1.3]

3.1 The right-hand side of step 2.1 is the characteristic function of the specified Borel probability $N(0,2Dt)$. Apply the reverse implication of [F8] to the Borel laws of $S_j$ to obtain weak convergence. The only non-finite-choice strength used here is the full AC explicitly carried by [F7]–[F9]; the finite product construction is in step 1.1 and its pointwise characteristic calculation is in step 2.1. [given, F7, F8, F9, step 1.1, step 2.1]

4.1 The walk limit in steps 1.1–2.1 concerns only fixed-time marginal laws under the stated independent-increment scaling; no path-space limit, deterministic collision limit, experiment, observed frequency, or empirical inference is part of the hypotheses or conclusion. [given, A1, A2, A3, step 1.1, step 2.1, step 3.1, step 1.2, step 1.3] ∎

items.statement: In the explicitly stipulated product model of [[pthm-csm-bernoulli-fluctuation-bounds]], take $n=100$ and $p=1/4$. We calculate model probabilities and bounds without supplying any observed trial results.
items.strategy:
**Proof technique:** direct.

**Given:** The model and hypotheses in the Example and [F1].

1.1 Substitution gives $\mathbb EK=25$ and $\operatorname{Var}(K)=100(1/4)(3/4)=75/4$. For $\varepsilon=1/10$, the Chebyshev bound is $(3/16)/(100/100)=3/16$, while the exponential bound is $2e^{-2}$. These are upper bounds on a specified model probability, not results from 100 recorded trials. [given, F1, algebra]

2.1 For $k=35$, $a=k/n=7/20$ and $$D(7/20\Vert1/4)=\frac7{20}\log\frac75+\frac{13}{20}\log\frac{13}{15}.$$ The point-mass estimate in [F1] therefore reads $$\frac1{101}e^{-100D(7/20\Vert1/4)}\le P_{1/4}(K=35)\le e^{-100D(7/20\Vert1/4)}.$$ This finite example displays the polynomial prefactor and common exponential rate without numerical fitting or empirical inference. [given, F1, algebra] ∎

items.statement: Specialize the finite-sector model of [[pthm-csm-nonadditive-phase-countermodel]] to $N=4$ at its positive transition parameter.
items.strategy:
**Proof technique:** direct.

**Given:** $N=4$, $\epsilon>0$, $\beta=\beta_c$, and $0\le\Delta<4\epsilon$.

1.1 Since $\beta_cN\epsilon=4\log2$, the three aggregate canonical sector weights are $1$, $e^{-4\log2}=1/16$, and $4^4e^{-8\log2}=1$. Thus $Z_4=33/16$ and $P_{\beta_c,4}(B_4)=(1/16)/(33/16)=1/33$. [given, F1, algebra]

2.1 The shell centered at $4\epsilon$ with half-width $\Delta<4\epsilon$ excludes the neighboring energy levels $0$ and $8\epsilon$, so it contains exactly the single state in $B_4$. Its uniform probability is therefore one on $B_4$, compared with the canonical value $1/33$. [given, F1, algebra] ∎
